eras.name: The Magic Mirror
eras.blurb: The very first photographs, made with silver, sunlight and patience.
eras.intro: Before 1826, nobody had ever seen a photograph. Then inventors in France and England found a way to make sunlight draw a picture. The first one took about eight hours to expose. A few years later, mirror-bright daguerreotypes and paper calotypes let people see their own faces — and the world — held perfectly still for the very first time.
eras.pr_note: Early cameras needed bright sun and long, still waiting.

eras.name: Glass, Wars & Faraway Places
eras.blurb: Wet glass plates carried to battlefields, mountains and far-off empires.
eras.intro: Photographers now coated glass plates with sticky chemicals, shot a picture, and developed it on the spot, often in a tent or a wagon. They hauled that darkroom to the Crimean War, the American Civil War, the Himalayas and Yosemite, and sent home pictures that made the big world feel real. Mathew Brady, Roger Fenton, Carleton Watkins, Julia Margaret Cameron and Eadweard Muybridge worked in this era.
eras.pr_note: Wet-plate photographers had to coat, expose and develop each glass plate within minutes.

eras.name: Everyone Gets a Camera
eras.blurb: Dry plates, roll film and the Kodak: photography leaves the studio.
eras.intro: Dry plates and then roll film meant you didn't have to be a chemist to take a photograph. In 1888 George Eastman's Kodak promised, "You press the button, we do the rest," and by 1900 a Brownie camera cost one dollar. Suddenly there were snapshots of families, city streets and fast-moving things, and reformers like Jacob Riis used photographs to show how others lived.
eras.pr_note: Dry-plate and roll film made quick snapshots possible.

eras.name: Photography Becomes Art
eras.blurb: Soft-focus dreams, sharp modern cities and the first color pictures.
eras.intro: Were photographs art? Alfred Stieglitz and his friends said yes. Some made soft, painterly pictures; others went for razor-sharp skyscrapers and close-ups of everyday things. The Lumière brothers' Autochrome and the Russian photographer Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky gave the world its first real color photographs, and the small, fast Leica camera was about to change everything.
eras.pr_note: Pictorialists used soft focus and special printing to make photographs look like drawings.

eras.name: The Camera Tells the Truth
eras.blurb: The Depression, the Second World War and the golden age of photo magazines.
eras.intro: During the Great Depression, the US government hired photographers like Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans to record hard times. Then came the Second World War, and magazines such as Life brought news pictures into every home. Photographs began to change what people believed and what laws they supported. This chapter has a few difficult images, shown with care.
eras.pr_note: Press photographers used fast 35mm cameras and flash bulbs.

eras.name: Color, Cities & the Moon
eras.blurb: Kodachrome, street photography and the first pictures of Earth from space.
eras.intro: Color film got cheaper, television and glossy magazines hungered for pictures, and photographers walked city streets looking for surprising moments. Then astronauts carried cameras to the Moon. In 1968 the Apollo 8 crew took a picture of Earth rising over the lunar horizon, and people saw their whole planet as one small, fragile marble.
eras.pr_note: Hasselblad cameras with color film went all the way to the Moon.

eras.name: The Digital Age
eras.blurb: Pixels, space telescopes and a camera in every pocket.
eras.intro: The first digital camera was built in 1975, and by the 2000s film was fading away. Today more photographs are taken every few minutes than were made in the entire nineteenth century. Space telescopes like Hubble and Webb use giant digital cameras to photograph galaxies billions of years old, and anyone with a phone can share a picture with the whole world in seconds.
eras.pr_note: A digital sensor turns light into numbers.

milestones.text: Nicéphore Niépce makes the oldest surviving photograph from his window in France. The exposure takes hours.
Louis Daguerre announces the daguerreotype. The word “photography” is coined the same year.
Robert Cornelius takes what's often called the first photographic selfie, in Philadelphia.
William Henry Fox Talbot patents the calotype: a paper negative you can print again and again.
Anna Atkins publishes the first book illustrated with photographs, using the cyanotype (blue) process.
Frederick Scott Archer's wet collodion process makes sharp glass negatives that can be copied.
Roger Fenton photographs the Crimean War, one of the first wars to be photographed.
The American Civil War begins; Mathew Brady's team and Alexander Gardner photograph it for the nation.
Eadweard Muybridge starts photographing galloping horses to settle a famous bet.
Muybridge's Horse in Motion shows that a galloping horse really does have all four hooves off the ground.
The first photograph is printed in a newspaper using the halftone process.
George Eastman launches the Kodak camera: “You press the button, we do the rest.”
Jacob Riis publishes How the Other Half Lives, using flash photographs of New York's poorest streets.
The $1 Brownie camera puts photography into children's hands.
The Lumière brothers sell Autochrome plates: the first practical color photographs.
Oskar Barnack builds the first Leica prototype, the model for small 35mm cameras.
Kodak introduces Kodachrome, a color film with rich, lasting colors.
The US government's Farm Security Administration begins photographing the Great Depression.
Life magazine launches and puts photographs at the center of the news.
Photographers including Robert Capa and Henri Cartier-Bresson found the Magnum agency.
Edwin Land's Polaroid camera produces a finished photograph in about a minute.
Apollo 8 astronauts photograph Earthrise over the Moon.
Apollo 11 astronauts take pictures of each other on the Moon.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson builds the first digital camera. It weighs eight pounds and records black-and-white pictures to a cassette tape.
Adobe Photoshop is released, and the Hubble Space Telescope is launched.
The first camera phones go on sale in Japan.
The iPhone arrives, and soon a good camera fits in every pocket.
The James Webb Space Telescope releases its first images of faraway galaxies.

n-niépce.bio: Nicéphore Niépce was a French inventor who made the oldest surviving photograph in 1826 by pointing a camera out of his window and waiting for hours. He did not live to see photography become popular, but his experiments started it all.

w-talbot.bio: William Henry Fox Talbot was an English scientist who invented photographs on paper made from a negative, so one picture could be printed again and again. He photographed his home at Lacock Abbey, books, flowers and lace, and called it the pencil of nature.

l-daguerre.bio: Louis Daguerre was a French painter of giant stage scenery who teamed up with Niépce and then perfected the daguerreotype, a mirror-bright photograph on silver. In 1839 France gave his invention to the world, and the age of photography began.

robert-cornelius.bio: Robert Cornelius was a Philadelphia lamp maker and chemist who took what is often called the first photographic self-portrait in 1839. He opened one of America's first photo studios the next year.

stam-stadsmuseum-gent.bio: STAM - Stadsmuseum Gent is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

d-hill.bio: David Octavius Hill was a Scottish painter who teamed up with the young chemist Robert Adamson in 1843. Together they made hundreds of lifelike portraits and scenes of fisherfolk, some of the first great artistic photographs.

louis-compte.bio: Louis Compte was a French priest and ship's chaplain who brought a daguerreotype camera to Rio de Janeiro in 1840 and took some of the first photographs made in South America.

armand-hippolyte-louis-fizeau.bio: Hippolyte Fizeau was a French physicist who measured the speed of light and made some of the first photographs of the Sun.

h-bayard.bio: Hippolyte Bayard was a French inventor who made direct positive paper photographs before anyone knew about Daguerre's. In 1840 he staged a famous picture of himself as a drowned man to protest not being credited as an inventor.

joseph-philibert-girault-de-prangey-s.bio: Girault de Prangey was a French artist who made hundreds of daguerreotypes of Mediterranean monuments in the 1840s.

henrik-cajander.bio: Henrik Cajander was a Finnish clergyman whose portrait was taken in the early years of photography.

c-marville.bio: Charles Marville was the official photographer of Paris, and recorded old crooked streets just before they were torn down to build wide boulevards. He also photographed the new streets, lamps and parks.

adolphe-braun.bio: Adolphe Braun began as a textile designer and became one of France's biggest photographers. He photographed the Alps in large prints and flower studies, and developed ways to print photographs in ink.

m-brady.bio: Mathew Brady ran photo studios in New York and Washington and took portraits of almost every important American of his day, including Abraham Lincoln. During the Civil War he sent teams of photographers to the battlefields.

deutscher-photograph.bio: Deutscher Photograph is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

vaillois.bio: Vaillois is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

samuel-j-miller.bio: Samuel Miller ran a photography studio in Akron, Ohio, and made some of the first portraits of Frederick Douglass.

g-gray.bio: Gustave Le Gray was a French painter and photographer who found ways to print dramatic skies and seas together, which was nearly impossible at the time. His seascapes are among the most admired of the 1850s.

platt-d-babbitt.bio: Platt Babbitt was the official photographer at Niagara Falls and sold daguerreotypes to visitors in the 1850s.

john-beasley-greene.bio: John Beasley Greene was an American archaeologist who lived in France and photographed the monuments of Egypt and Algeria in the 1850s. He died young, at 24, while traveling in Egypt.

maxime-du-camp.bio: Maxime Du Camp was a French writer who traveled up the Nile in 1849 with his friend, the novelist Gustave Flaubert, and photographed temples and statues on the way. His book of pictures from Egypt and Nubia was one of the first photographically illustrated travel books.

charles-nègre.bio: Charles Nègre was a French painter who turned to photography and photographed Paris street trades, Chartres cathedral and the south of France. He often hired models to pose as street musicians and chimney sweeps.

edouard-denis-baldus.bio: Édouard Baldus was a painter who became one of France's leading photographers. He made huge pictures of monuments and railways, and the government hired him to record the Louvre and the great floods of 1856.

n-w-pease.bio: N. W. Pease was a nineteenth-century photographer who sold stereo pictures of the Moon and landscapes.

southworth.bio: Albert Southworth and Josiah Hawes ran a famous daguerreotype studio in Boston from 1843 to 1862. They made large, lifelike portraits of poets, politicians and ordinary Bostonians.

rmn.bio: RMN is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

nadar.bio: Nadar was a Parisian cartoonist, balloonist and photographer. He made striking portraits of artists, writers and musicians, and took the first aerial photographs of Paris from a hot-air balloon.

thomas-martin-easterly.bio: Thomas Easterly was a daguerreotypist in St. Louis, Missouri. His portraits of Native American delegates and his rare daguerreotypes of the city's streets and riverfront are some of the earliest pictures of the American West.

robert-macpherson.bio: Robert MacPherson was a Scottish surgeon who settled in Rome and photographed its ruins and churches for visitors.

bisson-frères.bio: Louis-Auguste and Auguste-Rosalie Bisson were brothers whose Paris studio made huge pictures of cathedrals and mountains, including the first photograph from the top of Mont Blanc.

auguste-salzmann.bio: Auguste Salzmann was a French painter and archaeologist who photographed Jerusalem in 1854 to study its ancient monuments.

william-langenheim-frederick-langenheim.bio: William Langenheim / Frederick Langenheim is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

r-fenton.bio: Roger Fenton was a British photographer who traveled to the Crimean War in 1855 with a wagon darkroom. His calm, careful pictures of soldiers and camps are among the first war photographs.

linnaeus-tripe.bio: Linnaeus Tripe was a British army officer who photographed temples in India and Burma in the 1850s using large paper negatives.

rufus-anson.bio: Rufus Anson was a New York daguerreotypist who ran portrait studios in New York and Brooklyn in the 1840s and 50s.

f-beato.bio: Felice Beato traveled from India to China to Japan with his camera, making some of the first war and travel photographs of Asia. He hand-colored his prints so they looked even more lifelike.

francis-frith.bio: Francis Frith was an English photographer who traveled up the Nile in the 1850s with a wagon-sized darkroom. He later built one of the world's largest photography companies, selling views of towns and landscapes.

o-rejlander.bio: Oscar Rejlander was a Swedish-born photographer in England who made huge composite pictures and photographed Charles Darwin's studies of expressions.

etienne-carjat.bio: Étienne Carjat was a French caricaturist and photographer who photographed the writers and artists of Paris. His portraits of Baudelaire and Rimbaud are among the best known.

h-robinson.bio: Henry Peach Robinson combined several negatives into a single picture to look like a painting. His staged scenes were very popular in Victorian England.

j-cameron.bio: Julia Margaret Cameron got her first camera at age 48 as a gift from her daughter. She made dreamy, soft-focus portraits of famous Victorians and her neighbors, filling her henhouse with glass plates and her fingers with chemical stains.

andré-adolphe-eugène-disdéri.bio: Disdéri patented the carte de visite in 1854, a way to make eight small photographs on a single plate. It made portraits cheap and started a worldwide craze for collecting pictures of friends and celebrities.

alexander-hesler.bio: Alexander Hesler was a Chicago photographer who took a famous portrait of Abraham Lincoln in Springfield, Illinois, in 1860.

a-gardner.bio: Alexander Gardner was a Scottish-born photographer who worked for Brady and then set up his own studio. His pictures of Antietam and Gettysburg showed Americans what a battlefield really looked like. He also took some of the last portraits of Lincoln.

c-watkins.bio: Carleton Watkins carried a huge camera and heavy glass plates into Yosemite in the 1860s. His giant prints of waterfalls and cliffs helped convince Congress to protect the valley, one of the first steps toward national parks.

t-o-sullivan.bio: Timothy O'Sullivan photographed the Civil War, then joined government survey teams to the deserts and canyons of the West, hauling his cameras on mules and boats. His pictures look strangely modern.

s-bourne.bio: Samuel Bourne spent seven years photographing India and the Himalayas, carrying a tent darkroom and fifty porters. He made some of the most beautiful mountain photographs of the 1860s and 70s.

us-archives.bio: The US National Archives keeps pictures made by government photographers, including Ansel Adams's national park photographs and the EPA's Documerica project. Most are in the public domain.

g-barnard.bio: George Barnard was an American photographer who took pictures of Sherman's army and of Atlanta and Charleston during the Civil War. He also made some of the earliest photographs of Niagara Falls.

john-reekie.bio: John Reekie was a Scottish-born photographer who worked with Alexander Gardner in Washington and photographed battlefields after the Civil War.

jr-james-anderson.bio: Jr James Anderson is credited as the photographer of work held by Art Institute of Chicago.

w-jackson.bio: William Henry Jackson joined the 1871 Yellowstone expedition and took the first photographs that most Americans ever saw of its geysers. His pictures helped persuade Congress to make Yellowstone the first national park.

e-muybridge.bio: Eadweard Muybridge was an English photographer in California who used a row of cameras with trip wires to photograph a galloping horse. He proved all four hooves leave the ground and invented a way to show pictures in motion.

charles-soulier.bio: Charles Soulier was a French photographer who sold stereoscopic views of Paris and photographed the city after the fires of the Commune in 1871.

j-thomson.bio: John Thomson traveled through China and Southeast Asia in the 1860s and 70s, then returned to London to photograph street life there. His book Street Life in London is an early landmark of documentary photography.

p-emerson.bio: Peter Henry Emerson was a British doctor and photographer who wanted pictures to look the way the eye sees, a little soft at the edges. He photographed farmers, boatmen and marshes in the English countryside.

laton-alton-huffman.bio: L. A. Huffman was a photographer in Miles City, Montana, who photographed cowboys, Native people and the open range when it was still wild.

e-steichen.bio: Edward Steichen was a painter, photographer and museum curator. He made dreamy early art photographs, later fashion pictures, and in 1955 organized the famous exhibition The Family of Man.

george-kendall-warren.bio: George Kendall Warren ran a busy portrait studio in Boston and photographed many well-known people, including Frederick Douglass.

giorgio-sommer.bio: Giorgio Sommer was a German photographer in Naples who sold photographs of Pompeii, Vesuvius and Italian cities to travelers.

frederick-h-evans.bio: Frederick Evans was a London bookseller who became a master photographer of cathedrals. He waited for the best light and refused to retouch his prints.

albert-fernique.bio: Albert Fernique was a French engineer and photographer who recorded the building of the Eiffel Tower and the Statue of Liberty in Paris.

r-dayal.bio: Raja Deen Dayal became one of India's most famous photographers and official photographer to the Nizam of Hyderabad. He photographed palaces, rulers and ordinary scenes across central India.

a-stieglitz.bio: Alfred Stieglitz fought to have photography accepted as an art. He ran galleries and a magazine in New York, and his own pictures of snowy streets, skyscrapers and clouds helped make modern photography.

louis-emile-durandelle.bio: Louis-Émile Durandelle photographed big building projects in France, including the Eiffel Tower under construction in 1888.

j-riis.bio: Jacob Riis moved from Denmark to New York as a young man and became a newspaper reporter. He used flash photographs of crowded tenements to show how poor families lived, and helped persuade the city to build better housing.

eduard-uhlenhuth.bio: Eduard Uhlenhuth was a German court photographer who photographed royal gatherings in Coburg and Gotha.

unknown-authorunknown-author.bio: Unknown authorUnknown author is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

a-genthe.bio: Arnold Genthe was a German-born photographer in San Francisco who photographed Chinatown with a hidden camera and the great earthquake and fire of 1906. He later made portraits of dancers and celebrities.

c-white.bio: Clarence H. White was an American photographer and teacher who made gentle, poetic pictures of family and friends in light-filled rooms. His school trained many future great photographers.

f-w-taylor.bio: F. W. Taylor is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

e-atget.bio: Eugène Atget was a former actor who spent decades photographing the streets, shops and gardens of old Paris at dawn, when they were empty. Almost unknown in his lifetime, he is now seen as a founder of modern photography.

adolph-f-muhr.bio: Adolph F. Muhr is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

l-hine.bio: Lewis Hine was a teacher who used his camera to fight for children. He photographed kids working in mills, mines and factories, and his pictures helped make child labor illegal in the United States.

g-käsebier.bio: Gertrude Käsebier started photography at age 37 and became one of America's most successful portrait photographers. She is known for tender pictures of mothers and children and portraits of Native American performers.

e-curtis.bio: Edward Curtis spent thirty years photographing Native American communities across North America for his huge work The North American Indian. His pictures are beautiful but were often staged, so they must be viewed with care.

james-craig-annan.bio: James Craig Annan was a Scottish photographer who revived the work of David Octavius Hill and made rich photogravure prints of landscapes and portraits.

john-t-daniels.bio: John Daniels was a lifesaver at Kill Devil Hills who pressed the shutter on the Wright brothers' camera when their plane left the ground in 1903.

alvin-langdon-coburn.bio: Alvin Langdon Coburn is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

s-prokudin-gorsky.bio: Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky was a Russian chemist who took three black-and-white pictures through red, green and blue filters, then combined them into stunning color images. Between 1909 and 1915 he traveled across the Russian Empire, photographing people, churches and landscapes in color.

johan-viktor-beck.bio: Johan Viktor Beck was a Swedish photographer who made some of the first color Autochromes of Stockholm.

tadeusz-rząca.bio: Tadeusz Rząca was a Polish photographer and professor who made Autochrome color photographs of Kraków.

henry-essenhigh-corke.bio: Henry Essenhigh Corke was a British amateur who made beautiful family portraits and scenes with Autochrome color plates.

stéphane-passet.bio: Stéphane Passet was the first photographer sent out by the banker Albert Kahn for his Archives of the Planet. He traveled to India, Mongolia, China and elsewhere with color Autochrome plates.

helen-messinger-murdoch.bio: Helen Messinger Murdoch is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

frank-hurley.bio: Frank Hurley was an Australian photographer and adventurer who went on Antarctic expeditions with Douglas Mawson and Ernest Shackleton. He took famous pictures of the ship Endurance trapped in ice.

p-strand.bio: Paul Strand was an American photographer who helped shift photography from soft-focus pictures to sharp, modern ones, with close-ups of everyday objects, city streets and faces.

marcel-duchamp.bio: Marcel Duchamp was a French-American artist who invented the "ready-made," ordinary objects shown as art. He submitted Fountain to an exhibition in 1917.

the-library-of-congress.bio: The Library of Congress is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

frédéric-gadmer.bio: Frédéric Gadmer was a French photographer for Albert Kahn's Archives of the Planet who documented the Middle East and Europe after the First World War.

la-broad-irwin.bio: La Broad Irwin is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

louis-bachrach.bio: Louis Bachrach ran a portrait studio that photographed several US presidents and famous people, including Thomas Edison.

e-d-schött.bio: E.D. Schött is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

roger-dumas.bio: Roger Dumas photographed for Albert Kahn's Archives of the Planet, including treaties and delegations between the wars.

auguste-léon.bio: Auguste Léon was a French photographer who worked for Albert Kahn's Archives of the Planet, taking color Autochromes of people and places in France and around the world.

emmanuel-sougez.bio: Emmanuel Sougez was a French photographer who helped found the "new objectivity" style, making crisp, careful pictures of everyday things.

albert-kahn.bio: Albert Kahn was a French banker who paid photographers to take color pictures around the world, creating the Archives of the Planet, about 72,000 Autochromes.

w-evans.bio: Walker Evans photographed American farms, storefronts and families during the Depression in clear, plain pictures that influenced photographers for generations.

samuel-herman-gottscho.bio: Samuel Gottscho photographed New York's architecture, gardens and skyline for decades.

a-adams.bio: Ansel Adams was an American photographer famous for his sharp, glowing pictures of Yosemite and other national parks. He loved wild places so much that he spent much of his life helping to protect them.

state-library-of-new-south-wales-collect.bio: State Library of New South Wales collection is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

a-rothstein.bio: Arthur Rothstein was the first photographer hired for the government's Depression-era photo project. His pictures of dust storms in Oklahoma showed the whole country what the Dust Bowl looked like.

d-lange.bio: Dorothea Lange photographed families struggling during the Great Depression for the US government. Her picture Migrant Mother became the best-known image of the era, and she later documented the unfair imprisonment of Japanese Americans.

r-lee.bio: Russell Lee was a chemist and painter who became one of the photographers for the Farm Security Administration. He photographed farm families, small towns and workers in the American West and South.

berenice-abbott.bio: Berenice Abbott worked with Man Ray in Paris and championed Eugène Atget's pictures. When she returned to New York, she spent years photographing its changing streets for her book Changing New York.

sam-shere.bio: Sam Shere was a news photographer who photographed the Hindenburg disaster in 1937 from the landing field.

m-wolcott.bio: Marion Post Wolcott was one of the few women on the government's Depression-era photo team. She photographed farm workers, small-town life and the American South with a keen eye for light and contrast.

a-palmer.bio: Alfred Palmer was a photographer for the Office of War Information. He took color photographs of American factory workers building airplanes during World War II.

j-vachon.bio: John Vachon started at the Farm Security Administration as a messenger and became a photographer, traveling across America to take quiet, thoughtful pictures of towns and people.

g-parks.bio: Gordon Parks taught himself photography after seeing pictures in a magazine. He became the first Black photographer at Life magazine and made powerful pictures of segregation, poverty, and everyday life, as well as writing books and directing films.

e-bubley.bio: Esther Bubley photographed American life in the 1940s, including a famous series of bus trips across the country. She made ordinary people look interesting.

us-navy.bio: Navy photographers record ships, aircraft and people at work. Their pictures are in the public domain.

dennis-charles-oulds.bio: Dennis Charles Oulds is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

j-delano.bio: Jack Delano was born in Ukraine, grew up in Philadelphia, and photographed railroads and rural life in color for the US government. He later moved to Puerto Rico and made films and music.

joe-rosenthal.bio: Joe Rosenthal was an Associated Press photographer who took the famous picture of the flag raising on Iwo Jima in 1945 and won a Pulitzer Prize.

arnold-e-samuelson.bio: Arnold Samuelson was a US Army lieutenant who photographed the liberation of the Ebensee concentration camp in 1945.

victor-jorgensen.bio: Victor Jorgensen was a US Navy photographer who took one of the best-known V-J Day pictures in Times Square.

notes.bio: Notes is credited as the photographer of work held by Wikimedia Commons.

bob-sandberg.bio: Bob Sandberg was a photographer for Look magazine who photographed baseball stars and everyday American life.

imogen-cunningham.bio: Imogen Cunningham photographed plants, portraits and street scenes in California. She helped found the f/64 group and kept working into her nineties.

nasa.bio: NASA's astronauts, robots and space telescopes have been photographing space and Earth for more than sixty years. Its images are in the public domain, free to use.

photos.t: View from the Window at Le Gras
photos.why: This is the oldest photograph that still exists. Nicéphore Niépce set a camera in an upstairs window in France and let sunlight draw on a metal plate for hours. The roofs, a pear tree and a barn show up as blurry shapes, and the sun seems to light both sides because it moved while he waited.
photos.k: Look at the buildings. Why do you think there is light on both the left and the right side?

photos.why: This is the real metal plate Niépce used in 1826 or 1827. Under the right light you can find roofs and a chimney in the silvery smudges. The plate is so fragile that it is kept in a sealed case, and the picture above it is a version made to be easier to see.
photos.k: Can you find a straight line that might be a rooftop?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: William Henry Fox Talbot made pictures like this before his camera pictures worked. He laid a flower on paper coated with silver chemicals and let the sun print its outline. He called them photogenic drawings, meaning drawings made by light.
photos.k: Find the thin stem. Which parts of the flower look the palest?
photos.pr: Photogenic drawing, stabilized (fixed) in potassium iodide, potassium bromide or

photos.why: Two people sit close together in this small daguerreotype, a picture on a mirror-polished silver plate. Each daguerreotype is one of a kind, and you have to tilt it to see the image. They were kept in little cases to protect the silver.
photos.k: They had to sit very still. How long can you hold a smile without moving?

photos.cr: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: Constance Talbot sits in profile, her head outlined in soft shadow. Her husband, William Henry Fox Talbot, made pictures of her and his home, Lacock Abbey, while he was inventing paper photography.
photos.k: Which way is she looking? What might she have been thinking about while she sat so still?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Two men in top hats sit at a table, playing chess. Early paper photographs needed many seconds of exposure, so everyone had to hold still, which makes a quiet game like chess a good choice.
photos.k: Who do you think is winning?

photos.why: Louis Daguerre took this picture of a busy Paris street from his window. The exposure took minutes, so moving carriages and walkers vanished. One man stood still to have his boots shined, and he became probably the first person ever photographed.
photos.k: Find the man at the corner having his shoes polished. Where did all the other people go?

photos.why: Early photographs were small and precious, so they were kept in velvet-lined cases, like this one with three oval portraits. People carried them like tiny pictures of loved ones.
photos.k: What does a keepsake of yours look like? Where do you keep it?

photos.t: Abby Frances Snow, Age Two and a Half
photos.why: A little girl in a ruffled dress sits for a daguerreotype. Toddlers rarely stay still, so pictures of very young children from this time are rare and special.
photos.k: How do you think the photographer got a two-year-old to stay still?

photos.cr: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: Talbot printed real plants onto paper by laying them under glass in the sun. The pink color comes from the chemicals and from toning the paper. Each print is a perfect shadow of a living flower.
photos.k: Count the flower shapes. Which one is the biggest?

photos.why: Robert Cornelius, a lamp maker from Philadelphia, took this picture of himself outside his father's store. He took the lens cap off, ran into the frame and stood still for several minutes. It is often called the first photographic selfie.
photos.k: He wrote on the back, "The first light picture ever taken." What would you write on the back of your selfie?

photos.why: Buildings were perfect for early photography because they never moved. This daguerreotype shows old houses beside a canal in Ghent, Belgium, just after the process was shared with the world.
photos.k: Look at the windows. How many can you count?

photos.why: Hill and Adamson, a painter and a chemist in Scotland, made calotype portraits with strong light and shadow. Hill arranged poses the way he would in a painting.
photos.k: What do you think the two men are thinking about?

photos.why: Robert Cornelius opened one of the first photo studios in America in 1840. His sitter here, an elderly Philadelphia lawyer born in France, shows how photography started to become a business.
photos.k: What do you notice about the man's face? What would you ask him?

photos.t: Winter Trees Reflected in a Pond
photos.cr: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
photos.why: Talbot photographed bare trees mirrored in still water. It is a calm picture made of lines and reflections, and one of the earliest photographs taken just for its beauty.
photos.k: Can you find where the real trees stop and their reflections begin?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.t: The Oldest Family Photograph in Brazil
photos.why: A French priest named Louis Compte brought the daguerreotype to Rio de Janeiro in 1840. This picture of Colonel João José Carneiro de Mendonça and his family, made in 1841, is known as the oldest family photograph in Brazil.
photos.k: How many people are in the family? Who might be the oldest?

photos.why: A family traveling to see young Emperor Pedro II crowned in Brazil had this daguerreotype taken. The oldest woman, Maria Meis, is said to have been 111 years old.
photos.k: Count the generations from the oldest person to the youngest.

photos.why: A father and son in simple clothes lean together for a camera. Many early photographs were of rich people, so a portrait of ordinary country folk is a treat.
photos.k: What do you think the father is feeling?

photos.cr: Through prior purchase with Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: Hippolyte Bayard went up to Montmartre, then a village of windmills on the edge of Paris, and photographed an old mill. Today the hill is covered with cafes and the white Sacré-Cœur church.
photos.k: Find the windmill's sails. Which way is the wind blowing?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Bayard, one of photography's inventors, liked quiet corners. This plain garden chair, with its shadows, is a simple picture that makes you wonder who just got up.
photos.k: Who do you think was sitting here a minute ago?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 4 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-1850

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Early photographers made records of old buildings that were being repaired or torn down. Bayard photographed this house with its shutters and scaffolding in Paris.
photos.k: Count the shuttered windows.
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 13 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Montmartre was once covered in windmills that ground grain. Bayard photographed them from a field, years before artists and cafes arrived.
photos.k: How many windmills can you count?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 18 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: The Madeleine church in Paris looks like a Greek temple. Bayard framed its columns so they march into deep shadow, using the new camera to study light and geometry.
photos.k: Count the columns you can see.
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 21 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.t: Earliest Known Photograph of a Living Animal
photos.why: This daguerreotype, taken in Rome by Joseph-Philibert Girault de Prangey, is believed to be the earliest photograph of a living animal. The animal rests by a cart and stayed calm long enough for the exposure.
photos.k: Find the animal near the bottom of the picture. Why did it have to stay so still?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Talbot lined up his china on shelves and photographed it, and he suggested in his book The Pencil of Nature that photographs could help police identify stolen goods. It is one of the first pictures made to record a collection.
photos.k: Count the cups and jugs. How many different shapes can you find?

photos.cr: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: A broom leans in a sunlit doorway. Talbot turned a plain household corner into a picture, showing that photography could find beauty in everyday things.
photos.k: Why do you think he gave a broom such a grand title?

photos.cr: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: Talbot photographed a plaster bust many times in the sun. Statues never moved, so they were perfect first models, and he could show how light changes a face.
photos.k: Where does the light fall on the face? Where are the deepest shadows?

photos.why: Thomas Chalmers was a famous Scottish minister who helped found a new Church of Scotland in 1843. Hill and Adamson took portraits of its founders.
photos.k: What does his face tell you about him?

photos.why: Hill and Adamson photographed the fishing families of Newhaven, a village near Edinburgh. The women who sold the catch posed in their striped aprons, and the pictures show real working lives.
photos.k: What jobs do you think these people did every day?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: A boy in a tartan kilt stands for a calotype portrait by Hill and Adamson. Children had to be very patient in early photography.
photos.k: What do you think he was told to do while the camera worked?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Talbot photographed the great column in Trafalgar Square in London while workers were still building it. It is a rare record of a famous monument before it was finished.
photos.k: What do you see on the wooden scaffolding?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: A piece of lace is laid out so every thread shows. Talbot included it in his book as a way to show how a camera copies fine details perfectly.
photos.k: Find a flower pattern in the lace.

photos.cr: Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: A thatched haystack with a ladder leaning on it sits beside a farm. Talbot chose a scene from everyday country life, and the ladder makes you imagine the farmer climbing up.
photos.k: Where do you think the ladder leads?

photos.why: A woman in a lace cap and shawl sits beside a table, lit from the side. Hill and Adamson worked in a garden studio in Edinburgh, where sunshine made their exposures shorter.
photos.k: What details of her clothing can you spot?

photos.why: Anna Jameson was an Irish-born writer who wrote books about art and about women's lives. Hill and Adamson photographed her in a soft calotype portrait.
photos.k: What kind of book do you think she is thinking about writing?

photos.why: This round daguerreotype was made through a microscope. Within a few years of the invention, scientists were using photographs to record things too small to draw easily.
photos.k: What do you think is under the microscope?

photos.why: A Finnish man in a dark coat sits for a daguerreotype in about 1844. Before photography, only wealthy families could afford painted portraits, and now many more people could have their faces saved.
photos.k: What does his serious look tell you about the time?

photos.t: A Young Woman in a Daguerreotype
photos.why: A young woman looks calmly at the camera in this daguerreotype from around 1850. The mirror-bright metal plate makes the picture seem to float.
photos.k: Imagine she is looking at you. What might she say?

photos.why: On the left is a dried fern, on the right a blue cyanotype of a fern. John Herschel invented the cyanotype in 1842, and it is the process behind blueprints.
photos.k: How are the real fern and its blue print alike? How are they different?

photos.why: Hill and Adamson photographed members of Scottish church councils. Men gather close around a book, which meant they all had to stay still for several seconds.
photos.k: What do you think they are reading?

photos.why: A Scottish doctor and diplomat who served in Persia, now seated for a Hill and Adamson calotype. Their soft, grainy portraits look like drawings in charcoal.
photos.k: What would you ask a man who had traveled so far?

photos.cr: Gift of Drs. William and Martha Heinemann-Pieper
photos.why: Charles Marville, the official photographer of Paris, photographed the new park at the edge of the city. The still water and tall trees mirror each other in a calm scene.
photos.k: Where do the trees end and their reflections begin?

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Cows are driven through a village street between half-timbered houses. Adolphe Braun, a photographer from Alsace in France, loved to record country life and used it to make prints for sale.
photos.k: How many cows can you count?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.why: Andrew Jackson, the seventh president of the United States, was photographed at his home near Nashville a few months before he died. It is one of the earliest photographs of an American president.
photos.k: What do you notice about his face and his stern look?

photos.why: A studio showed off its skill with a wall of tiny daguerreotype portraits of all sorts of people, young and old. Photographers hung displays like this in shop windows to attract customers.
photos.k: Which portrait do you like best?

photos.why: A woman of the fishing village of Newhaven, near Edinburgh, sits in her striped skirt and shawl. Hill and Adamson photographed these fish sellers, and their pictures became some of the best-known early photographs.
photos.k: What do you think she carries in her basket?

photos.t: The Cannon Mons Meg at Edinburgh
photos.why: Mons Meg is a huge medieval cannon at Edinburgh Castle that once fired stone balls. A guard stands beside it, so you can see how enormous it is.
photos.k: How tall is the guard compared with the cannon?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Hippolyte Bayard photographed a narrow street in Paris, with tall houses on one side and a quiet curve ahead. It shows the city before the wide boulevards were built.
photos.k: Find the chimney pots on the rooftops.
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 16 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.why: A Romanian historian and revolutionary leader sits for a portrait in Paris in 1846. He helped lead an uprising in Wallachia two years later.
photos.k: What do you think he is dreaming of?

photos.why: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish writer and historian whose books were read all over the English-speaking world. This daguerreotype shows him as a serious man in a dark coat.
photos.k: What would you ask a historian?

photos.why: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery as a young man and became one of the greatest speakers and writers in American history. He believed photographs showed Black Americans as dignified people, and he sat for more portraits than any other American of his century.
photos.k: He looks right at you. What do you think he wants you to feel?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Bayard photographed the oldest standing bridge in Paris, the Pont Neuf, with riverside houses and barges. The view looks much as it did centuries before, and today.
photos.k: Find the boats along the river.
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 14 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed this old abbey church with its tall spire for the French government, which sent photographers to record historic buildings that needed repair. It was one of the first photo projects for protecting heritage.
photos.k: How tall is the spire compared with the church?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: In February 1848, Parisians built barricades in the streets and overthrew their king. Bayard photographed the Rue Royale just after the fighting, with paving stones torn up and a few barricades left.
photos.k: What do you think happened here a few days before?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 12 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.why: Platt Babbitt was the official photographer at Niagara Falls and sold daguerreotypes to tourists. It is one of the earliest photographs of the great waterfall.
photos.k: What sounds do you imagine you would hear here?

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: John Beasley Greene was an American working in Egypt who photographed the Great Sphinx half buried in sand. At the time, the Sphinx was covered up to its shoulders, and you can see the pyramid beyond.
photos.k: How much of the Sphinx is buried in sand?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.why: Maxime Du Camp traveled up the Nile with the writer Gustave Flaubert and photographed what he found. This mosque with its slim minaret stands at the edge of old Cairo.
photos.k: Find the minaret. What does it look like?

photos.why: Du Camp photographed the Sphinx straight on, with the pyramids behind. His pictures made Egypt look real to people who might never travel there.
photos.k: Imagine standing where the camera stood. What would you see around you?

photos.why: An ancient Egyptian temple on the Nile, half ruined and filled with sand. Du Camp's pictures helped Europeans fall in love with Egypt's past.
photos.k: How many columns can you count?

photos.why: Four tall columns stand in the desert in Nubia, a region of the upper Nile. Du Camp carried his camera and glass plates by boat and camel to reach places like this.
photos.k: How would you carry delicate glass plates across a desert?

photos.why: Du Camp photographed a gigantic statue of Pharaoh Ramses II at Abu Simbel and had a man stand by to show its scale. The statue is partly buried in sand, with a tiny figure at the right.
photos.k: Find the person. How big is the statue compared to him?

photos.t: Path in the Forest of Fontainebleau
photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed sun and shade on a forest path near Paris, where painters also went to paint. His soft paper prints show light the way an artist would.
photos.k: Where does the path lead?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.why: Edgar Allan Poe, who wrote spooky poems and stories like The Raven, was photographed in 1849, the last year of his life. The picture is a copy of a daguerreotype.
photos.k: Poe wrote about ravens and mysteries. What story would you tell with a face like this?

photos.why: Le Gray photographed an old tree growing between rocks in Fontainebleau Forest. The picture has deep shadows and bright patches, almost like a painting.
photos.k: How would you describe the tree's shape?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in memory of her mother Kathleen W. Harvey
photos.why: A group of street musicians stands in a Paris courtyard, each in worn clothes. Charles Nègre posed them to look natural, which was difficult when exposures took many seconds.
photos.k: What instruments do you think they played?
photos.pr: Photogravure, from the portfolio "Charles Negre: Treize Heliogravures, 1854–1857

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray found a way to print both a dark sea and a bright, cloudy sky, which was almost impossible at the time. This steam tugboat on the horizon is one of his famous seascapes.
photos.k: What time of day do you think it is?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by William Mares
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed a rocky valley in France where a new railroad was going to run. He was hired to photograph railways and monuments, and he made them look grand.
photos.k: Where could a train run through this valley?

photos.why: Two almost identical pictures of the full moon sit side by side, made for a stereoscope. The first photographs of the Moon were made in the 1840s and 50s, and they showed people its craters for the first time.
photos.k: Can you spot dark patches on the Moon? Those are the lunar seas.

photos.why: Albert Southworth and Josiah Hawes ran the most famous daguerreotype studio in Boston. Their sitters look natural instead of stiff, and this woman in profile, with her hair swept neatly back, shows their quiet style.
photos.k: What can you tell about her from the way she holds her head?

photos.why: Early film saw blue sky as white, so clouds almost disappeared. Gustave Le Gray found ways to print a dramatic cloudy sky, sometimes using a separate negative, and made some of the first great sky pictures.
photos.k: What shapes can you see in the clouds?

photos.why: In 1851 the French government sent five photographers on the Mission Héliographique to photograph historic buildings that needed protecting. Le Gray photographed the great church of Saint-Sernin and its tall octagonal tower.
photos.k: How many levels can you count in the tower?

photos.why: A French doctor named Duchenne used gentle electric currents to make a man's face muscles move so he could study expressions. He found that a real smile uses the muscles around the eyes, which is now called a Duchenne smile. Charles Darwin used his photographs in a book about emotions.
photos.k: Try a fake smile and then a real one. Can you feel your eyes squeeze in the real one?
photos.pr: Albumen print from glass plate negative

photos.why: Le Gray photographed the old walls and towers of the medieval city of Carcassonne in France when they were crumbling. They were restored soon afterward, so pictures like this show the town before repairs.
photos.k: Count the round towers you can see.

photos.why: Thomas Easterly's daguerreotype shows a pond on the edge of St. Louis, Missouri, with horse-drawn wagons along the shore. The pond was drained and built over not long afterward.
photos.k: What would you see here today if you stood in the same place?

photos.t: Fourth and Olive Streets, St. Louis
photos.why: On a corner in St. Louis in 1851, awnings shade the shop windows and a horse-drawn wagon waits in the street. It is one of the earliest photographs of an American city street.
photos.k: What are the people and horses doing?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in memory of her mother Kathleen W. Harvey
photos.why: Théophile Gautier was a French poet and novelist who believed that beauty was reason enough for art. Charles Nègre photographed him as a thoughtful man with a beard.
photos.k: What do you think he is looking at?
photos.pr: Photogravure, from the portfolio Charles Negre: Treize Heliogravures, 1854–1857

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: According to legend, a nymph named Egeria met an ancient Roman king in this shady grotto and gave him advice. Robert MacPherson, a Scottish doctor living in Rome, photographed its mossy stones and trees.
photos.k: Why do you think people made up a story about a magical cave?

photos.why: This triumphal arch in the south of France was built about two thousand years ago. Édouard Baldus photographed it with huge paper negatives, so every carved detail shows.
photos.k: How many archways does it have?

photos.why: In the 1850s and 60s, Paris was torn apart and rebuilt with wide boulevards and tall stone buildings. Charles Marville photographed the new streets in the early morning, with long exposures that left them empty.
photos.k: Why do you think there are no people in the picture?

photos.why: The Bisson brothers photographed the carvings over the doors of Chartres Cathedral, with Jesus seated in the middle and rows of small figures below. Their sharp pictures let people study the carvings without climbing up.
photos.k: How many figures can you find carved above the door?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Reproductions photographiques des plus beaux type

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Lucia Woods Lindley and Daniel A. Lindley, Jr.
photos.why: Huge carved columns rise at Medinet Habu in Egypt, a temple built for Pharaoh Ramses III more than three thousand years ago. John Beasley Greene was one of the first photographers to carry cameras up the Nile.
photos.k: How many people holding hands would it take to go around one column?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in memory of her mother Kathleen W. Harvey
photos.why: Auguste Salzmann photographed tombs carved in rock near Jerusalem to prove they were very old. His careful pictures were published in a large book and helped start the study of the city's ancient past.
photos.k: Find the doorways carved in the cliff.

photos.why: A smiling woman in a dark dress stands in a Boston studio. Southworth and Hawes asked their sitters to relax, and it shows.
photos.k: What do you think made her smile?

photos.why: William and Frederick Langenheim, brothers in Philadelphia, photographed the partial solar eclipse of May 1854 with a daguerreotype. The Sun shows as a thin crescent with the Moon covering the rest. Taking a picture of the Sun without damaging the camera was a challenge.
photos.k: Why do you think the Sun looks like a crescent? What is covering the other part?

photos.why: Thomas Easterly, a daguerreotypist in St. Louis, photographed the busy riverside streets of his city from rooftops. This view shows shops, signs and a growing town.
photos.k: Read the signs. What do you think each shop sold?

photos.t: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
photos.why: Roger Fenton named this road in Crimea after a Bible verse. Soldiers were fighting nearby, and cannonballs lay all over the ground. Fenton made two versions, one with cannonballs on the road and one without, and historians still argue which came first.
photos.k: The road is bare in this version. Where do you think the cannonballs went?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.why: Graves of British officers who died in the Crimean War are marked with white stones on a bare hillside. Fenton's photographs were shown in London so the public could see what war was like.
photos.k: How does an empty hillside make you feel?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.why: Lord Raglan, the British general, sits with other commanders outside a farmhouse, planning their next moves. Fenton was one of the first photographers to travel to a war zone, with a horse-drawn darkroom wagon.
photos.k: Who do you think is giving the orders?

photos.t: A Quiet Day in the Mortar Battery
photos.why: Fenton's cameras were too slow to photograph fighting, so he photographed calm moments, like soldiers resting beside their heavy mortars. These pictures made the war look more peaceful than it really was.
photos.k: Which parts of a war can a camera not show?
photos.pr: Salted paper print,  from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Soldiers gather in thick coats beside a hut in the Crimean winter. Fenton's pictures showed families at home that their sons were surviving cold and mud.
photos.k: What would you wear in a cold camp like this?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 40 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.why: Adolphe Braun photographed the snowy Alps and sold his prints to travelers as souvenirs. He ran one of the largest photography businesses in France.
photos.k: Which peak do you think is the highest?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: A paddle steamer glides on a Swiss lake with mountains behind. Braun's careful pictures made travel look elegant.
photos.k: Where do you think the steamer is heading?

photos.cr: Through prior purchase with Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: Linnaeus Tripe joined a British mission to Burma in 1855 and photographed the temples of Pagan (Bagan), where thousands of temples rise from the plains. He printed large pictures on paper that show every carving.
photos.k: How many pointed shapes can you count on this temple?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Burma Views" (1857)

photos.t: The Tomb of the Christian Woman, Algeria
photos.why: A great round tomb with a stepped roof stands near Algiers. It was built long ago for a king and queen of Mauretania, but local people told stories of a Christian woman buried within.
photos.k: What shape does the tomb remind you of?

photos.why: A dog sits upright in a chair in a photo studio, as if it were a member of the family. Pets were hard to photograph, but families wanted to remember them too.
photos.k: What do you think the dog was waiting for?

photos.why: A sailing brig drifts on a calm sea beneath dramatic clouds. Gustave Le Gray was famous for seascapes like this, made by combining two negatives so both sea and sky looked right.
photos.k: What kind of weather does the sky suggest?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.why: The sun is a bright glow behind clouds and shines onto the sea. Le Gray was one of the first photographers to capture the sun's light directly, and people were amazed.
photos.k: Try to find where the sun reflects on the water.
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Elena Urschel; through prior gifts of Mr. Arnold Crane, David C. and Sarajean Ruttenberg, Max McGraw, and Reva and David Logan
photos.why: In 1856, the Rhône river flooded southern France. Édouard Baldus photographed fields turned into lakes, with trees and houses standing in the water.
photos.k: What would you do if your street became a river?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean and Julien Levy
photos.why: Gustave Doré was a French artist famous for illustrating the Bible and Dante's Inferno. Nadar, his friend, photographed him as a relaxed young man with a scarf.
photos.k: What do you think he drew in his sketchbook?

photos.t: The Dome of the Rock, Jerusalem
photos.why: The golden Dome of the Rock has shone over Jerusalem for more than 1,300 years. Felix Beato photographed the city from the Mount of Olives side, with the old walls in front.
photos.k: Find the dome. What do you notice about the wall in front?

photos.t: Ships in the Harbor at Sète
photos.why: Tall masts and rigging fill a French Mediterranean harbor. Le Gray made the ships crisp and the sky soft, so the picture feels almost like a painting.
photos.k: How many masts can you count?
photos.pr: Albumen print, No. 10 from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.why: Francis Frith carried a wagon-sized darkroom up the Nile and photographed ancient temples. A few columns remain standing here in the sunny sand.
photos.k: What happened to the rest of the temple?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 5 from the album "Egypt and Palestine, Volume I" (1858)

photos.t: Osiride Pillars and the Fallen Colossus
photos.why: In Thebes, Frith photographed huge pillars carved with the pharaoh and the broken statue of Ramses II, the king called Ozymandias in a famous poem.
photos.k: How big do you think the fallen statue was?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 17 from the album "Egypt and Palestine, Volume I" (1858)

photos.why: Le Gray waited for a stormy day to photograph a huge wave breaking on the shore. He added a sky from a different negative, because the camera could not capture both well in one exposure.
photos.k: Does this look like a calm day or a stormy one?
photos.pr: Albumen print, No. 17 from the Vistas del Mar album

photos.t: The Sphinx and the Great Pyramid
photos.why: Francis Frith photographed the Sphinx with the Great Pyramid rising behind it. The pyramid is about 4,500 years old, and the Sphinx was half buried in sand when he took this.
photos.k: How much of the Sphinx can you see above the sand?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Egypt, Palestine, Nubia" (1862)

photos.why: Oscar Rejlander combined thirty separate negatives into one huge picture about choosing between good and bad paths in life. Some people were shocked by the figures, others called it a masterpiece. Queen Victoria bought a copy.
photos.k: Why would a photographer need thirty negatives for one picture?

photos.why: Charles Baudelaire was a French poet who wrote Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil). Étienne Carjat photographed him about 1863 looking calm and a little stern, and the picture became the best-known portrait of the poet.
photos.k: What do you think a poet thinks about while sitting for a picture?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the periodical “Galerie Contemporaine Littéraire, Artistique”

photos.t: She Runs Home and Tells Her Mother
photos.why: Henry Peach Robinson set up scenes like a theater director, with models and props, and sometimes joined several negatives. In this country kitchen, a young girl rushes in with news for her mother.
photos.k: What news do you think she is telling?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.t: Small Mosque in the Kaiserbagh, Lucknow
photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
photos.why: Felice Beato photographed the palaces of Lucknow, India, soon after the great uprising of 1857. The domed mosque in the royal garden is shown with its arches and minarets.
photos.k: Find the dome. How many smaller towers are around it?

photos.why: In 1857 Napoleon III's army camped at Châlons in France. Le Gray photographed officers resting beside a tent, as part of a project to record the emperor's soldiers.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a tent camp like this?

photos.why: Julia Margaret Cameron brought her camera close to her models' faces and used soft focus. People complained that her pictures were blurry, but she wanted to catch the feeling of a person, not every detail.
photos.k: How does the soft focus change the way her face looks?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in honor of Katherine Bussard
photos.why: In 1854 André Disdéri patented a way to take many small pictures on one plate and cut them into cards. These cheap cartes de visite sparked a craze for collecting portraits of friends and celebrities. This sheet shows the guitarist Napoléon Coste in several poses.
photos.k: Which pose do you like best?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Alexander Hesler photographed Lincoln in Springfield, Illinois, while he was running for president. Soon after, an eleven-year-old girl wrote to suggest that he'd look better with a beard, and he grew one.
photos.k: What do you think Lincoln would look like with a beard?

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed this narrow old Paris street before it was torn down to build wide new roads. It was here in 1610 that King Henry IV was killed in his carriage.
photos.k: How wide is the street? Could a modern car fit?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Gift of Michael Mattis and Judith Hochberg
photos.why: British and French troops attacked the Taku forts in China in 1860, during the Second Opium War. Felice Beato followed the army and photographed the broken walls soon afterward.
photos.k: What do the broken walls tell you about what happened?

photos.why: Beato followed the British army to Beijing and photographed the gates and towers of its walls. They were some of the first photographs most Europeans ever saw of the Chinese capital.
photos.k: How tall do you think the wall is?

photos.t: Streets and Shops in the Tartar City
photos.why: Painted wooden shopfronts with tall signs line a street in Beijing in 1860. Beato's pictures show daily life as well as battles.
photos.k: What do you think each shop sold?

photos.why: In 1860 Japan sent its first official embassy to the United States, and the delegates in silk robes were mobbed by curious crowds. Alexander Gardner photographed three of them in Washington.
photos.k: What do you think they thought of America?

photos.why: Mathew Brady photographed Lincoln on the day he gave a speech at Cooper Union in New York. Prints of this portrait spread across the country, and Lincoln later said that Brady and that speech had helped make him president.
photos.k: What do you notice about his clothes and expression?

photos.why: Giuseppe Garibaldi was an Italian general who led volunteers to unite Italy. Le Gray photographed him in 1860, the year Garibaldi conquered Sicily.
photos.k: Why do you think people followed him?

photos.why: Oscar Rejlander staged this scene in his studio to show how people felt when work was scarce. A man leans his head on his hand beside a workbench. Rejlander often used models and costumes to tell a story.
photos.k: Is this a real moment or a staged one? How can you tell?

photos.t: Inside the North Fort at Taku
photos.why: Felice Beato photographed this broken fort in China just after British and French forces captured it in 1860. Timber ladders and ruined walls show how hard the fighting was.
photos.k: What do you think happened to the wooden platform?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by the Kunstadter Family Foundation
photos.why: Carleton Watkins hauled his camera and glass plates by mule to Yosemite. Three years later, President Lincoln signed a law to protect the valley, and photographs like this helped people see why.
photos.k: Look for the tall pointed rocks. Why do you think they are called spires?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by the Kunstadter Family Foundation
photos.why: This stereo view shows a tall rock column in Yosemite. It was named for the Swiss scientist Louis Agassiz, who studied glaciers. Two nearly identical pictures side by side make a 3-D image when seen through a stereoscope.
photos.k: Can you spot any difference between the left and right pictures?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by the Kunstadter Family Foundation
photos.why: Watkins photographed the Merced River so still that the mountain doubles in the water. The huge granite wall of El Capitan was famous even then.
photos.k: Which half is the real mountain and which half is the reflection?

photos.why: In 1861, as the Civil War began, Mathew Brady photographed Union generals relaxing on a porch. Brady wanted to record the whole war, and he spent a fortune doing it.
photos.k: Who looks the most important to you?

photos.why: Soon after the beard suggestion, Lincoln let his whiskers grow. Mathew Brady photographed him in 1861, and prints were sold across the country.
photos.k: How is this Lincoln different from the one in the 1860 portrait?

photos.why: Soldiers of the 1st Connecticut Artillery stand beside big cannons at a fort that helped defend Washington, D.C. Mathew Brady's team photographed the early days of the Civil War.
photos.k: How many cannons can you see?

photos.why: In September 1862, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War was fought around this stone bridge at Antietam. Alexander Gardner photographed it only a few days later.
photos.k: The bridge is calm. Does it look like a place where a battle happened?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 20 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.why: Alfred Tennyson was the poet laureate of Britain who wrote The Charge of the Light Brigade. Oscar Rejlander photographed him with deep shadows on his face, as if posed for a painting.
photos.k: If you wrote poems, what would you write about?

photos.why: In October 1862, President Lincoln visited General McClellan's tent at Antietam. He wanted the army to move faster, and Alexander Gardner photographed the meeting.
photos.k: Who is the tall man in the tent?

photos.why: Timothy O'Sullivan photographed soldiers who had died in the fields of Gettysburg a couple of days after the battle. This picture and others like it showed the public the true cost of war.
photos.k: Why do you think photographers showed such hard scenes?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 36 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.why: When the Confederate government fled Richmond in April 1865, fires destroyed much of the city. Gardner photographed the burned arsenal, with cannonballs stacked at the foot of the broken wall.
photos.k: How many cannonballs can you see in the pile?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 91 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.t: Slaughter Pen, Foot of Round Top
photos.why: At Gettysburg, O'Sullivan photographed the rocky ground near Little Round Top, where soldiers had fought. The photographs were shown in galleries so people could see what battles left behind.
photos.k: Why would some people want to see such pictures, while others turn away?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 44 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.why: Gardner's team photographed a dead soldier in a rocky nook at Gettysburg. Later, researchers found the same body in another picture that was taken about forty yards away, which shows the photographers moved him to get a better scene.
photos.k: If a photograph is staged, can it still tell the truth?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 40 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.why: O'Sullivan photographed the woods where General John Reynolds was killed on the first day of the Battle of Gettysburg. The scattered bodies show how the fight swept across the field.
photos.k: Why did photographers return to battlefields after a fight?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 37 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.why: Alexander Gardner titled this picture of a dead soldier among rocks, which was later shown to be staged: the same body appears in another photograph where he had been carried to a different spot.
photos.k: What can you learn about trusting photographs from this story?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 41 from the album "Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the

photos.why: Charles Darwin, who explained evolution in On the Origin of Species, visited Julia Margaret Cameron in 1868. He later said he liked her photograph of him better than any other taken of him.
photos.k: What does his face tell you about his thoughts?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean Levy and the Estate of Julien Levy
photos.why: Nadar, a photographer and balloonist, built a giant balloon called Le Géant in Paris in 1863 with a basket the size of a small house. He hoped to raise money for flying machines.
photos.k: How many people can you count? How big is the balloon compared with them?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver printing out paper print

photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
photos.why: Samuel Bourne photographed Shimla, a town in the Himalayan foothills where British rulers escaped the summer heat. He used a tent as a darkroom and had porters carry his equipment.
photos.k: What would it take to carry glass plates through the mountains?

photos.t: Shimla, View of the Church from Mount Jakko
photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
photos.why: Snow covers pine trees on the hillside in Shimla. Bourne carried his camera through bitter weather to catch scenes like this.
photos.k: How many trees are covered in snow?

photos.why: Union army railroad crews rebuilt bridges destroyed in the Civil War so quickly that Lincoln joked one was made of beanpoles and cornstalks. Photographs of the U.S. Military Railroad show how much engineering lay behind the war.
photos.k: How would you build a bridge in a few days?

photos.why: Lewis Carroll, whose real name was Charles Dodgson, wrote Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. He was also a keen photographer, and here the photographer Oscar Rejlander captured him in a relaxed pose.
photos.k: What do you think inspired Alice's wonderland?

photos.why: Alexander Gardner photographed Abraham Lincoln on November 8, 1863, eleven days before the president gave the Gettysburg Address. The portrait was made into small cabinet cards that people bought and collected.
photos.k: What do you notice about his tired, serious face?

photos.why: George Sand was a French novelist who wrote under a man's name and wore trousers when most women did not. Nadar photographed her in a soft light, wrapped in a large cloak.
photos.k: Why might a woman choose a man's name for her books?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the periodical “Galerie Contemporaine Littéraire, Artistique”

photos.t: Rebel Works in Front of Atlanta
photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: George Barnard followed General Sherman's army and photographed Atlanta's earth fortifications, with a cannon and a tent behind. His photographs were published in a large album of Sherman's campaign.
photos.k: What do you think happened to the trees?
photos.pr: Albumen print, plate 42 from the album "Photographic Views of the Sherman Campai

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Julia Jackson was Julia Margaret Cameron's niece and one of the most photographed beauties of her day. She later became the mother of the writer Virginia Woolf and the painter Vanessa Bell.
photos.k: What do you think she is thinking about?

photos.why: Sarah Bernhardt, then about twenty, became one of the greatest actresses in the world, known as the Divine Sarah. Nadar photographed her in a dark gown with her face turned in profile.
photos.k: How does she hold her head?

photos.why: Sojourner Truth escaped slavery and became a famous speaker for freedom and women's rights. She sold cards like this one to earn money, with the line "I sell the shadow to support the substance."
photos.k: What do you think she meant by shadow and substance?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Edward Byron Smith
photos.why: The Grizzly Giant is an ancient sequoia tree in Yosemite's Mariposa Grove. Watkins had men stand next to it to show how enormous it was, and photographs like this helped win protection for the trees.
photos.k: How many people stand next to the tree? How big does it make them look?

photos.t: First View of the Yosemite Valley
photos.cr: Laura T. Magnuson and Maurice D. Galleher Endowments
photos.why: Watkins photographed the valley from the edge of a cliff, with El Capitan and Bridal Veil Fall across it. This became the classic view, and photographers have returned to it ever since.
photos.k: Which cliff do you think is El Capitan?

photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. James Ward Thorne
photos.why: People nicknamed this portrait of the poet Tennyson "the Dirty Monk" because of his shaggy hair and dark cloak. Julia Margaret Cameron's dramatic close-ups made her sitters look like heroes from legends.
photos.k: Does he look like a monk, a poet or a wizard?
photos.pr: Photogravure, plate 3 from the album "Lord Tennyson and his Friends" (1893)

photos.why: John Reekie photographed soldiers collecting remains from the battlefield at Cold Harbor, Virginia, after the war. It is a hard picture to look at, but it made people think about the price of war.
photos.k: Why do you think the photographer went back to a battlefield?

photos.t: Ruins of the Pinckney Mansion, Charleston
photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Charleston, South Carolina, where the Civil War began, was battered by fire and cannon fire. George Barnard photographed its ruined buildings in 1865, as the war ended.
photos.k: What would you want to rebuild first?
photos.pr: Albumen print, plate 59 from the album "Photographic Views of the Sherman Campai

photos.t: Ruins of the Railroad Depot, Charleston
photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Tall chimneys stand in the empty shell of a burned station. Barnard's photos show how much of the South lay in ruins.
photos.k: How many chimneys can you count?
photos.pr: Albumen print, plate 61 from the album "Photographic Views of the Sherman Campai

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed this narrow old Paris street before it was changed for good. Wet cobblestones, shuttered shops and tall houses make it feel like another century.
photos.k: Does this look like a street you would like to walk down?

photos.why: Inside the world's largest church, a giant bronze canopy stands under a huge dome. James Anderson photographed Rome for visitors who could not travel there.
photos.k: Look at the people. How big is the canopy compared with them?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: General William Tecumseh Sherman sits with his commanders at the end of the Civil War. George Barnard photographed Sherman's army, and this portrait shows the men who led it.
photos.k: Which one do you think is Sherman?
photos.pr: Albumen print, plate 1 from the album "Photographic Views of the Sherman Campaig

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean Levy and the Estate of Julien Levy
photos.why: Édouard Manet was a French painter who helped begin modern art. Nadar, who was friends with many artists and writers, photographed him as a thoughtful young man.
photos.k: What do you think he saw when he looked at his own paintings?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the periodical “Galerie Contemporaine Littéraire, Artistique”

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Bridal Veil Fall drops about 620 feet down a cliff in Yosemite. Watkins made huge prints on glass plates the size of a small table, so people in cities felt as if they stood in the valley.
photos.k: What sound do you think the waterfall makes?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.why: William Henry Jackson photographed two great peaks in southern Colorado. Before cameras, most Americans could only imagine what the West looked like.
photos.k: What do you think the weather is like up there?

photos.why: Queen Victoria loved photography. She and Prince Albert collected thousands of photographs. André Disdéri, the cartes-de-visite king, photographed her in a dark dress.
photos.k: Why do you think she liked collecting photographs?

photos.t: Julia Jackson in an Oval Frame
photos.cr: Gift of David C. and Sarajean Ruttenberg
photos.why: Cameron photographed her niece Julia Jackson in an oval, with her face close up and soft. Cameron said she wanted pictures that showed the beauty of a person's thought.
photos.k: How does the soft focus change how you feel about her?

photos.why: In 1867 Cameron photographed her niece with her hair loose around her shoulders. Women in Victorian times usually wore their hair up, so this was a bold, artistic choice.
photos.k: Why do you think the hair is loose?
