photos.why: John Herschel was an astronomer who helped invent photography. He came up with the words photography, negative and positive and discovered how to fix pictures so they would not fade. Cameron photographed him as an old man with wild white hair.
photos.k: Why do you think a scientist's hair looks like that?

photos.why: Timothy O'Sullivan traveled with government surveyors across the deserts of the West. Here a wagon team crosses the sand dunes, tiny beside the hills of sand.
photos.k: How would you cross a desert like this?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Long before his famous horse pictures, Eadweard Muybridge photographed Yosemite under the Greek name "Helios," which means the Sun. His pictures of the tall waterfall made people dream of visiting.
photos.k: How tall do you think the falls are compared with the trees?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Julia Margaret Cameron staged scenes from the Bible and legends, using friends and neighbors as models. Soft focus and dramatic light make this picture of an angel feel like a painting.
photos.k: Which parts of the picture look blurry, and why might Cameron want that?

photos.why: Cameron borrowed the look of a famous Italian painting of Beatrice Cenci for this portrait. A young woman looks out from under a headcloth, with her eyes soft and thoughtful.
photos.k: Do you think the woman looks happy, sad or both?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean Levy and the Estate of Julien Levy
photos.why: In the fall of 1870, Paris was surrounded by an enemy army. The city sent mail out by balloon, and Le Neptune lifted off from Montmartre on September 23. Nadar, the balloonist and photographer, organized balloon flights during the siege.
photos.k: What would you put in a balloon mailbag?

photos.why: Alexandre Dumas wrote adventures such as The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo. Étienne Carjat photographed him in a studio portrait showing his curly hair and generous smile.
photos.k: Which Dumas story would you most like to read?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the periodical “Galerie Contemporaine Littéraire, Artistique”

photos.why: In 1871 William Henry Jackson joined an expedition to Yellowstone and photographed its geysers. The next year Congress made Yellowstone the first national park, and photographs like this helped persuade lawmakers.
photos.k: What do you think the geyser sounds like?

photos.t: The Paris Fire, Hôtel de Ville
photos.why: In May 1871, during the Paris Commune uprising, fires destroyed the city hall of Paris. Charles Soulier photographed the empty, burned shell of the building.
photos.k: Why would people want to remember a burned building?

photos.why: Oscar Rejlander photographed Charles Darwin, the scientist who explained evolution, seated in profile with his big white beard. Rejlander also took photographs for Darwin's book about emotions.
photos.k: What do you think Darwin is thinking about?

photos.t: Valley of the Yosemite from Rocky Ford
photos.why: Muybridge photographed Yosemite's cliffs and the Merced River in the 1870s. The mirrored water makes the valley seem twice as big.
photos.k: What do you notice in the reflections?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.why: Charles Darwin used photographs by Oscar Rejlander in his 1872 book about how people and animals show feelings. These faces show laughing, crying and surprise. It was one of the first science books to use photographs.
photos.k: Make each face yourself. Which emotions are easiest to show?

photos.t: Ancient Ruins in the Cañon de Chelly
photos.why: Timothy O'Sullivan photographed a stone house tucked in a canyon wall in Arizona, built about 800 years ago by the ancestors of the Pueblo people. He lowered himself on ropes and used long exposures to catch it.
photos.k: Why would people build homes high up in a cliff?

photos.why: El Morro in New Mexico is a rock where travelers carved their names for hundreds of years, from Spanish explorers to settlers. O'Sullivan laid a ruler against the rock to show the size of the inscriptions.
photos.k: Where would you carve your name, and what would you write?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Geographical & Geological Explorations & Surveys

photos.why: Julia Margaret Cameron moved with her husband to Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) in 1875. Her photographs there show women standing close together in the shade, one balancing a pot.
photos.k: What do you think they were carrying?

photos.why: John Thomson photographed the people who worked on London's streets, from clowns to chimney sweeps, for his book Street Life in London. It is one of the first books to show ordinary working people in photographs.
photos.k: What kind of job is it to be a street clown?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the album "Street Life in London"

photos.why: A street seller with a donkey cart calls out her berries on a London street. John Thomson and the writer Adolphe Smith made Street Life in London to show the people who earned a living on the streets.
photos.k: How would you advertise fresh strawberries if you were selling them in the street?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the album "Street Life in London"

photos.why: "Crawlers" was a name for the poorest people of London, often elderly women who had no work and wandered the streets. Thomson's photographs made readers see the people behind the word.
photos.k: Why might a picture change how you feel about someone?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the album "Street Life in London"

photos.t: When the Day's Work Is Done
photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Lucia Woods
photos.why: Henry Peach Robinson arranged this cozy cottage scene with models. A family gathers around a table in warm light at the end of a working day, like a painting made with a camera.
photos.k: What do you think each person is doing after a long day?

photos.why: Some families lived and traveled in wooden wagons, moving through London and the English countryside. John Thomson photographed them in front of their caravan for Street Life in London.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a wagon?

photos.why: Porters in London's Covent Garden market carried heavy baskets of fruit and vegetables on their heads. Thomson photographed them taking a break.
photos.k: How heavy do you think the baskets were?

photos.why: Thomas Edison invented the phonograph, a machine that could record and play back sound, in 1877. This photograph was taken in Mathew Brady's Washington studio after Edison stayed up all night showing it off.
photos.k: What would you record on a phonograph?

photos.why: Peter Henry Emerson photographed farm life in Norfolk, England, with a cart piled with hay beside the trees. He wanted photographs that looked the way the human eye sees, a bit soft around the edges.
photos.k: What time of year do you think it is?
photos.pr: Photogravure, Frontispiece from "Pictures of East Anglian Life," published by Sa

photos.why: Eadweard Muybridge lined up cameras along a racetrack so a galloping horse tripped the shutters one after another. The twelve pictures show the horse, Sallie Gardner, with all four hooves off the ground at once.
photos.k: Look at the horse's legs. When are all four hooves off the ground?

photos.why: Leland Stanford, a rich California governor, bet that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves off the ground. Muybridge proved him right with his photographs, and they also helped inspire the first movies.
photos.k: Do the horse's legs look the way painters usually showed them?

photos.why: Eadweard Muybridge photographed San Francisco's big new buildings from above. The wide streets and awnings show a city growing fast after the Gold Rush.
photos.k: What do you see on the street below?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Douglas Kenyon
photos.why: L. A. Huffman lived in Miles City, Montana, and photographed Native people, cowboys and the great plains. This portrait of a Cheyenne woman, her braids neatly hanging, was made when the old ways of life on the plains were changing quickly.
photos.k: What do you notice about her clothes and hair?

photos.why: James Nasmyth was a Scottish engineer who invented the steam hammer and made careful drawings of the Moon. Hill and Adamson photographed him resting his head on his hand, as if deep in thought.
photos.k: What might an inventor be thinking about?

photos.why: Edward Steichen was one of the first artists to try Autochrome, the first practical color process. Women in light summer dresses lounge on a veranda, and the soft colors look like an Impressionist painting.
photos.k: What colors do you notice? How does it feel to see old photographs in color?

photos.why: Frederick Douglass was a leader in the fight to end slavery and win equal rights. In this portrait taken around 1879, he is in his sixties with a full white beard and a calm gaze.
photos.k: What does his steady look tell you?

photos.t: Plaster Cast of a Body, Pompeii
photos.cr: Gift of W. Bruce and Delaney H. Lundberg
photos.why: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, ash buried the city of Pompeii. Later, archaeologists poured plaster into the hollows left by bodies, creating casts like this one. Giorgio Sommer photographed them for visitors.
photos.k: How can an empty space in ash tell us what a person looked like?

photos.cr: Gift of Arielle Kozloff Brodkey in memory of Dr. Jerald S. Brodkey
photos.why: Frederick H. Evans photographed English cathedrals, waiting hours for the light to be just right. He printed on platinum paper, which gave soft, silvery grays, and refused to touch up his pictures.
photos.k: How does the light make the stone look?

photos.why: A farmer guides two horses pulling a plow across a big field under a gray sky. Peter Henry Emerson wanted to show the strength and beauty of working life in the English countryside.
photos.k: How do you think the farmer and horses feel at the end of the day?
photos.pr: Photogravure, plate IV from "Pictures of East Anglian Life," published by Sampso

photos.why: Two boys stop on a path in the marshes of Norfolk to look at a toad. Emerson's photographs from East Anglia caught everyday moments of country life.
photos.k: What would you do if you found a toad on your path?
photos.pr: Photogravure, pl. XXVII from the album "Pictures of East Anglian Life" (1888)

photos.t: The Head of the Statue of Liberty
photos.why: In Paris, the giant head of the Statue of Liberty stood in a yard while the rest of the statue was built. The statue was later taken apart and shipped to New York in crates.
photos.k: How tall are the people standing beside the head?

photos.why: The Kailasa temple in India was carved out of a single hillside of rock, from the top down. Raja Deen Dayal photographed its carved columns and towers.
photos.k: How could people carve a whole temple out of one rock?

photos.why: Men carry bundles of reeds home across the marshes of the Norfolk Broads. Emerson made soft-focus pictures like this to show the beauty of a vanishing way of life.
photos.k: What did people use reeds for?
photos.pr: Platinum print, pl. I from the album "Life and Landscape on the Norfolk Broads"

photos.why: Two people gather water lilies from a small boat among the reeds of the Norfolk Broads. Emerson's pictures of this watery landscape became famous and made photographers think about how the eye really sees.
photos.k: What do you think they will do with the lilies?
photos.pr: Platinum print, pl. IX from the album "Life and Landscape on the Norfolk Broads"

photos.why: Workers on the Norfolk Broads pole a flat boat loaded with marsh hay. Peter Henry Emerson published this picture in a book of photographs of East Anglian life.
photos.k: What do you think the hay was used for?
photos.pr: Platinum print, pl. XVII from the album "Life and Landscape on the Norfolk Broad

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean Levy and the Estate of Julien Levy
photos.why: The chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul turned a hundred in 1886, and Paul Nadar, Nadar's son, photographed him as he talked. The pictures were published with his words in a newspaper, the first photo-interview ever.
photos.k: What would you ask someone who is a hundred years old?

photos.why: Paul Nadar's series of Chevreul gesturing and speaking was printed with captions of his words. It was the first time a newspaper used photographs to tell an interview, and it is the grandfather of today's video interviews.
photos.k: Which of his expressions do you like best?

photos.why: A road lined with bare trees runs into the distance on a cold day. Alfred Stieglitz was a young student in Germany when he made this quiet picture and began to love photography.
photos.k: What season does it feel like?

photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed wide stone steps leading down to the water in Chioggia, Italy. The sunlight and smooth stone make a simple, calm picture.
photos.k: Where do you think the steps lead?

photos.cr: Gift of Phyllis Seltzer in memory of John Cook
photos.why: Muybridge photographed horses and other animals at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1880s and published hundreds of plates as Animal Locomotion. Each row of small pictures shows a horse moving a step at a time.
photos.k: Count the frames. Which one shows a hoof on the ground?

photos.why: This plate from Animal Locomotion shows a bison walking, step by step. Muybridge photographed animals at the Philadelphia Zoo, and artists and scientists used his plates to study how bodies move.
photos.k: How does the buffalo's head move as it walks?

photos.why: A big family gathers on a porch and steps at Lake George, New York. Alfred Stieglitz's family owned a summer home there, and it later became his favorite place to photograph.
photos.k: How many people can you count?

photos.why: Louis-Émile Durandelle photographed the Eiffel Tower as its iron legs rose above Paris. It was finished in March 1889 and was the tallest structure in the world, at about 300 meters.
photos.k: How many levels does the tower have so far?

photos.why: Jacob Riis photographed a narrow alley in New York's Mulberry Bend, one of the roughest slums in the city. He used flash powder, which produced a sudden bang and light, so people in his pictures often look startled.
photos.k: What do you notice about the people's faces?

photos.t: Baby in a Slum Tenement Hallway
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A baby crawls on the floor in a hallway of a crowded New York tenement. Riis's pictures showed readers that children were growing up in dark, cramped buildings.
photos.k: What would you change about this hallway?

photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed a young woman writing at a table beside a window, with the sunlight forming stripes. It was one of his first pictures to win notice, and it shows that a photographer can paint with light.
photos.k: Where does the sunlight fall in the room?

photos.why: In this crowded tenement room in New York's Bayard Street, lodgers paid five cents a night for a spot to sleep on the floor. Jacob Riis made the picture with flash powder, and it helped convince New Yorkers to improve housing.
photos.k: How many people can you spot sleeping in the room?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Families from Bohemia (now part of the Czech Republic) rolled cigars at home in their tiny New York apartments, working for very little pay. Riis photographed them in their cramped kitchen workroom.
photos.k: What would it be like to work where you live?

photos.t: Sweatshop in a Ludlow Street Tenement
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Men, women and children sewed clothes in crowded rooms, often for long hours. Riis's pictures of sweatshops showed the hidden work behind the clothes people bought.
photos.k: What can you tell about their jobs from the room?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A family gathers in a dark basement room in a poor corner of New York called Poverty Gap. Jacob Riis wrote that the room was damp and dim, and that children lived there year-round.
photos.k: What would you want for this family?

photos.t: A Street in Sterzing, the Tyrol
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed a narrow street in an old Austrian town, with bright sun on one side and deep shadow on the other. The line between light and dark gives the picture its mood.
photos.k: Where would you walk to stay in the shade?

photos.why: Raja Lala Deen Dayal was one of India's most famous photographers, appointed to photograph the Nizam of Hyderabad. This portrait shows him in a white turban, calm and confident.
photos.k: What would a photographer need to carry around India in the 1880s?

photos.why: Frederick H. Evans photographed the carved doorway of Ely Cathedral in England, with a tiny figure standing inside. He loved cathedrals and waited for the best light, and he never touched up his pictures.
photos.k: How does the small person make the doorway feel bigger?

photos.cr: Gift of Daniel, Richard, and Jonathan Logan
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed a narrow Venetian canal, where houses and boats double in the water. Reflections became one of his favorite subjects.
photos.k: Where does the building end and its reflection begin?

photos.why: On a snowy day in New York, a driver blankets his horse at the end of the streetcar line. Alfred Stieglitz took this picture with a hand camera in a storm, and it became one of the first great photographs of city life.
photos.k: What are the horses wearing to keep warm?

photos.why: A woman in a white cap mends fishing nets on the dunes of the Dutch coast. Stieglitz traveled around Europe in the 1890s photographing ordinary people at their work.
photos.k: What jobs do people do at the sea?

photos.why: Mountain peaks rise above a sea of cloud and snow in the Alps. Stieglitz photographed Europe's mountains while he traveled as a young man.
photos.k: How would you climb a mountain like this?

photos.t: A Wet Day on the Boulevard, Paris
photos.why: Rain makes the Paris street shine like glass. Stieglitz loved bad weather, which other photographers avoided, and he showed that rain, mist and snow could be beautiful.
photos.k: What do you notice about the wet street?

photos.why: Two people in long shawls hurry along a Dutch beach toward a church as the weather turns. Stieglitz photographed this on a trip to the Netherlands.
photos.k: What do you think they are hurrying away from?

photos.why: Queen Victoria sits with dozens of her children, grandchildren and their families. Several became kings and queens in other countries, which is why people called her the grandmother of Europe.
photos.k: How many people can you count in the picture?

photos.why: Alexander Graham Bell was born in Scotland and invented the telephone in 1876. He also taught deaf children to speak and spent his life inventing.
photos.k: What would you ask someone who invented the telephone?

photos.why: Arnold Genthe photographed San Francisco's Chinatown with a hidden camera, because many people there feared cameras. In this picture, a woman and children take a stroll in their holiday best.
photos.k: Why might some people have been afraid of cameras?

photos.cr: Gift of John Flory, Elizabeth Flory Kelly, and Phoebe Flory
photos.why: Clarence H. White photographed his wife by a window, with soft light on her profile. He and his friends believed a photograph could be gentle and poetic.
photos.k: What might she see outside?
photos.pr: platinum print with watercolor and gouache

photos.t: A Merchant and His Servant, Chinatown
photos.why: A Chinese merchant in a long robe poses with a younger attendant in San Francisco's Chinatown. Genthe made hundreds of pictures of the neighborhood before the 1906 earthquake destroyed it.
photos.k: What do their clothes tell you about their roles?

photos.cr: Gift of John Flory, Elizabeth Flory Kelly, and Phoebe Flory
photos.why: Two women sit close, absorbed in a book by the window. Clarence H. White arranged simple scenes of family life in soft light.
photos.k: What book do you think they are reading?

photos.why: Leo Tolstoy wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina, two of the most famous novels ever. Although he was born a rich count, he often wore a plain peasant's blouse, as in this portrait.
photos.k: Why would a rich man wear peasant clothes?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Eugène Atget photographed the shops and streets of old Paris. This corner shop with its sign and displays is a small piece of vanished city life.
photos.k: What kinds of things do you think this shop sold?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Special Photography Acquisition Fund
photos.why: A street musician pushes his hand organ down a Paris lane. Atget made hundreds of pictures of street trades, for artists who wanted to record everyday Paris.
photos.k: What kind of music do you think he played?

photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed bare trees and a path by streetlights in a freezing night. It took long exposures and patience, and the soft glow makes the park look like a winter dream.
photos.k: What sounds would you hear in a park on a freezing night?

photos.t: Mount of the Holy Cross, Colorado
photos.why: William Henry Jackson photographed this peak, where snow fills the cracks in the shape of a cross. In the 1890s his company used a Swiss process called photochrom to add color to black-and-white photographs, and postcards like this were a sensation.
photos.k: Find the cross on the mountain.

photos.why: Geronimo was an Apache leader who fought for years to protect his people's homeland. At the time of this portrait, he was a prisoner of war and was taken to an exposition in Omaha, Nebraska, where he was photographed.
photos.k: What do you read in his face?

photos.why: Lewis Hine photographed children working in cotton mills across the American South. This tiny girl stands among the huge spinning machines. His pictures helped convince Americans to pass laws against child labor.
photos.k: How old do you think she is? How would you feel working in this mill?

photos.cr: Gift of Daniel, Richard, and Jonathan Logan
photos.why: Gertrude Käsebier posed a mother in white and her daughter in dark clothes in a doorway. The picture, named for a line from the Bible, made her famous when it was shown at galleries.
photos.k: Why do you think one is dressed in white and the other in black?

photos.why: Käsebier's The Manger shows a mother and child bathed in soft light, like a modern Madonna. She believed photographers could make pictures as moving as paintings.
photos.k: How do the soft light and white dress change the mood?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Special Photography Acquisition Fund
photos.why: A woman carries a big basket of bread on a Paris street. Eugène Atget photographed street workers, and the pictures became a record of old Parisian jobs.
photos.k: What other jobs on the street do you know about?

photos.why: A man walks a Paris lane with lampshades piled on his arm. Atget photographed people who sold things on the street and sold his prints to artists, who used them as references.
photos.k: How many lampshades can you see?

photos.why: Nikola Tesla sits calmly while artificial lightning crackles from his giant coil in Colorado Springs. The photograph is a double exposure: he sat in one shot, and the sparks were added in another, since he would not have survived real lightning that close.
photos.k: Why do you think they used a double exposure?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: Edward S. Curtis photographed a huge circle of tipis on the prairie during a Piegan sun dance gathering. He spent thirty years documenting Native American communities.
photos.k: Why would so many families gather together on the prairie?
photos.pr: Photogravure, plate 192 from "The North American Indian, Volume 6" (1911)

photos.why: James Craig Annan, a Scottish photographer, made soft, dark prints of the castle on its rock. He used a printing method called photogravure, which gave rich, velvet-like tones.
photos.k: How does the castle look against the sky?

photos.why: In a gentle snowstorm, horse-drawn carriages move along Fifth Avenue in New York. Stieglitz made the picture soft, like a painting, and printed it in a way that glowed.
photos.k: What is moving along the street? What isn't moving?

photos.why: A slim young tree stands on a wet New York street in a soft mist of rain. Stieglitz loved to photograph weather, and he used it to make the picture look like a drawing.
photos.k: Does it feel like a happy rain or a sad one?

photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed the sculptor Auguste Rodin in front of his famous statue The Thinker. In the dark, Rodin's shadow seems to join the statue.
photos.k: Which one is the sculpture and which is the sculptor?

photos.why: Gertrude Käsebier photographed members of Buffalo Bill's Wild West show when they came to New York. Amos Two Bulls, a Lakota man, is shown in a dignified profile, in a picture that looks like a painting.
photos.k: What do you think he is looking at?

photos.why: A steam locomotive moves out of a rail yard in New York in smoky light. Stieglitz showed that machines and cities could be as beautiful as landscapes.
photos.k: What do you hear when a train passes?

photos.why: A girl holds a bowl of fruit in this color photograph. The Lumière brothers began selling Autochrome plates in 1907. They used tiny dyed grains of potato starch as color filters, and Stieglitz was one of the first artists to try them on his daughter Kitty.
photos.k: How are the colors different from the colors in a modern photo?

photos.why: Gertrude Käsebier photographed her friend and fellow photographer Alfred Stieglitz in 1902, the year he founded the Photo-Secession, a group that fought to make photography respected as an art.
photos.k: What does his face say about a man who was determined?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Gaylord Donnelley
photos.why: Edward S. Curtis photographed the adobe houses of Zuni Pueblo in New Mexico, stacked like steps with ladders to the upper levels. The pueblo has been lived in for hundreds of years.
photos.k: How would you get up to the top floor?
photos.pr: Photogravure on vellum, from "The North American Indian"

photos.why: Stieglitz photographed the new Flatiron Building in a snowfall, its triangular shape rising behind a bare tree. He said it looked like the bow of a ship moving toward him.
photos.k: Do you see why people compared the building to a ship?

photos.why: Chief Joseph, a Nez Perce leader, led his people on a long, desperate journey in 1877 to avoid being forced onto a reservation. Edward Curtis photographed him in 1903, the year before he died.
photos.k: What do you think he is thinking about?

photos.why: On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew the first powered airplane for twelve seconds and 120 feet. A man named John Daniels pressed the shutter of a camera aimed at the plane just as it left the ground, while Wilbur ran alongside.
photos.k: Find the person running at the right. Who do you think it is?

photos.cr: Acquired through exchange with George Eastman House
photos.why: Lewis Hine photographed an immigrant mother and her children at Ellis Island. Hine named it after paintings of Mary and the baby Jesus, to show that these families deserved respect.
photos.k: What do you think this mother hopes for her children?

photos.why: Edward Steichen made this picture of a moonlit pond in New York by printing it in layers of green and blue pigment. It was one of the first photographs to sell for a high price.
photos.k: Can you find the reflections of the trees?

photos.t: Laborers at Work on the Panama Canal
photos.why: In 1904 the United States began building a canal across Panama to link the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Thousands of workers, many from the Caribbean, dug through mountains in the hot sun.
photos.k: What tools do you think they used?

photos.why: Edward S. Curtis photographed Navajo riders walking across the floor of a canyon in Arizona, tiny compared with the tall red cliffs. The picture is one of his most famous.
photos.k: How tall do you think the cliffs are compared with the riders?

photos.why: Richard Strauss was a German composer who wrote the music that opens the film 2001: A Space Odyssey. Edward Steichen photographed him in dramatic shadow.
photos.k: What kind of music do you think he would write?

photos.why: Steichen photographed the Flatiron Building in rainy twilight, and printed it in blue-green tones with a few touches of color. The picture feels like a painting of a misty New York evening.
photos.k: What time of day does it feel like?

photos.cr: Acquired through exchange with George Eastman House
photos.why: A boy in a cap breaks into a big grin. Lewis Hine photographed working children across the US, and often caught their personalities as well as their hard lives.
photos.k: What do you think made him smile?

photos.cr: Acquired through exchange with George Eastman House
photos.why: On a hot New York day, a baby sleeps on a cushion outside while an old man rests by the wall of a tenement. Crowded apartments were so stuffy that families took their children out into the street.
photos.k: Where do you like to go when it's too hot at home?

photos.why: Lewis Hine photographed new arrivals at Ellis Island, where about twelve million immigrants entered the United States. This young woman wears a headscarf and an open, serious expression.
photos.k: What do you think she hoped to find in America?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: A family sits together on a bench in the great hall at Ellis Island, waiting to learn whether they can enter the country. Hine treated each family as individuals.
photos.k: What would you pack if you were moving to another country?

photos.why: A family stands near piles of luggage at Ellis Island, looking for their lost bags. Hine's pictures show that arriving in a new country was hard.
photos.k: What would be the first thing you'd look for?

photos.why: The French sculptor Auguste Rodin made The Thinker and many other famous statues. Gertrude Käsebier photographed him in Paris with his white beard glowing against a pale background.
photos.k: What kind of things would a sculptor see in a block of stone?

photos.why: H. G. Wells wrote science fiction classics such as The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds. Alvin Langdon Coburn photographed him with his chin resting on his hand, as if thinking about the future.
photos.k: What would you invent if you could travel in time?

photos.why: Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky took three black-and-white pictures of the same scene through red, green and blue filters, and combined them into a color image. This field of poppies is one of his early color experiments.
photos.k: How do the three filters help show true colors?

photos.why: Prokudin-Gorsky traveled to Switzerland and photographed a mountain lake in color. Few people had ever seen real color photographs like this, a century ago.
photos.k: What colors surprise you most?

photos.why: A vase of white flowers sits on a bright red tablecloth. Prokudin-Gorsky used still lifes to test his color process, since a still life does not move between the three exposures.
photos.k: Why is a still life easier for his method than a street scene?

photos.why: A group of newsboys stand in the shadow of the Brooklyn Bridge with stacks of newspapers. Hine's pictures showed that many boys worked long hours selling papers in city streets.
photos.k: What time of day do you think they started work?

photos.why: On April 18, 1906, a huge earthquake and the fires that followed destroyed much of San Francisco and killed about three thousand people. This view of the ruins shows block after block flattened.
photos.k: What would it be like to see your city like this?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: Hollow Horn Bear was a Lakota leader who served as a scout and a chief. Edward Curtis photographed him in 1907, and his face later appeared on a US postage stamp.
photos.k: What can you tell about him from his face?
photos.pr: Photogravure, plate 82 from "The North American Indian, Volume 3" (1908)

photos.why: On a ship crossing to Europe, Alfred Stieglitz looked down from the first-class deck at passengers in the cheaper steerage section. He rushed to get his camera and had one plate left. The shapes of the gangway, funnel and straw hat make a picture that helped begin modern photography.
photos.k: Find the straight lines and the round shapes. How do they fit together?

photos.t: Frank Eugene Seated at a Table
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz made some of the first color photographs in America with Autochrome plates. Here his friend Frank Eugene, a photographer and painter, sits at a table with flowers and glasses.
photos.k: Do the soft colors feel like a painting?

photos.why: A girl in a straw hat and striped dress leans sideways in the sun in this Autochrome by Stieglitz. The glowing pink and blue come from tiny grains of colored starch.
photos.k: How is it different from a black-and-white portrait?

photos.cr: Acquired through exchange with George Eastman House
photos.why: Sadie Pfeifer, a young girl, stands at a spinning frame in a South Carolina cotton mill. Lewis Hine compared children's heights with his coat buttons to estimate how old they were. His photographs helped end child labor.
photos.k: How would you feel working in a mill instead of going to school?

photos.why: In coal mines, trapper boys sat alone in the dark and opened and closed doors to let cars through. They sometimes worked ten hours a day. Hine photographed boys like this one in West Virginia.
photos.k: How would you spend ten hours in the dark?

photos.why: Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky took this color portrait of the famous writer Leo Tolstoy sitting in a garden at his estate in 1908. It is one of the first color photographs of a major writer.
photos.k: What does it feel like to see someone from over a century ago in color?

photos.why: Mark Twain, the author of Tom Sawyer, liked to write in bed. This Autochrome shows him in a red robe, reading with white hair against the pillow.
photos.k: What book would you read in bed?

photos.why: Boys who worked in an Indiana glassworks pose in front of the factory. Lewis Hine photographed child workers and kept notes of their names and ages, hoping to show that laws were needed.
photos.k: How old do you think the youngest boy is?

photos.why: Boys work through the night in a glass factory, where a furnace glows in the dark. Hine sometimes sneaked into factories pretending to be a salesman, so he could photograph the working children.
photos.k: Why do you think the boys worked at night?

photos.why: Alvin Langdon Coburn photographed the tall rigging of a ship reflected in the water so it forms a web of lines. He wanted pictures to be as beautiful as paintings and prints.
photos.k: Can you find the ship's masts and their reflections?

photos.cr: Acquired through exchange with George Eastman House
photos.why: A girl holds a baby on her hip. In many poor families, older children took care of their little brothers and sisters while the grown-ups worked. Lewis Hine photographed families in Pittsburgh for a big study of working-class life.
photos.k: Do you help care for younger children?

photos.why: Three coal miners with lamps on their caps stand together. Hine photographed men who had spent decades underground in Pennsylvania, so people above ground could see who dug the coal.
photos.k: What would it feel like to work in the dark every day?

photos.why: Dozens of boys stand in front of a Pennsylvania coal breaker, where they picked slate from moving coal for hours. The sharp coal cut their fingers. Hine's photographs were used to push for laws against child labor.
photos.k: How many boys can you count?

photos.why: A Welsh coal miner looks upward with the lamp on his cap shining. Hine called the picture "Follow the Gleam," because a miner's lamp was his only light underground.
photos.k: Where do you think his lamp is shining?

photos.t: Newsies at Skeeter Branch, St. Louis
photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Charles and Ruth Levy Foundation
photos.why: Boys sell newspapers on a city street. Some of these newsboys were only ten or eleven years old and had already learned grown-up habits. Hine hoped his pictures would show how hard these children's lives were.
photos.k: What would you do if you were a newsboy?

photos.t: On the Shore of the Lake, Kutenai
photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: A Kutenai person stands beside a canoe with an unusual pointed shape, called a sturgeon-nose canoe, on a lake shore. Edward Curtis photographed many peoples of the Pacific Northwest.
photos.k: What do you notice about the shape of the canoe?
photos.pr: Photogravure, plate 251 from "The North American Indian, Volume 7" (1911)

photos.why: Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky photographed a sunny path through a tall pine forest in color. The trees glow gold and green, much as they would for someone standing there more than a hundred years ago.
photos.k: What would it smell like in this forest?

photos.why: Addie Card was twelve years old when Lewis Hine photographed her at a cotton mill in North Pownal, Vermont. She stands barefoot beside the spinning frames, looking right at the camera. Her face became a symbol of the fight against child labor.
photos.k: What do you think she was thinking when she looked at the camera?

photos.why: Green domes of a Russian church rise above a town on a river in this color photograph by Prokudin-Gorsky. He traveled across the Russian Empire for years, photographing it in color for the tsar.
photos.k: Why do you think he chose to photograph a church?

photos.why: Johan Beck made this color picture of Stockholm's royal palace at twilight, with a boat gliding past. Color photographs were brand new, and the soft hues give the scene a dreamy look.
photos.k: What time of day do you think it is?

photos.why: Tadeusz Rząca photographed the red-brick Collegium Novum, a building of Poland's Jagiellonian University, in color. He used Autochrome, the first practical color process.
photos.k: How many arches can you find?

photos.why: Sergey Prokudin-Gorsky photographed Alim Khan, the emir of Bukhara, in a bright blue robe covered in medals. The vivid color shows how bold the clothing of Central Asia was.
photos.k: What colors stand out? How do you think they looked in life?

photos.why: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and then returned many times to lead others to freedom along the Underground Railroad. In this photograph she is an elderly woman in a white dress, near the end of her long life.
photos.k: What do you admire most about someone who risked her life for others?

photos.why: Soldiers fought here in a sunken road at the Battle of Antietam in September 1862. Alexander Gardner photographed the bodies still lying there two days later, and his pictures, shown in New York, were among the first to show Americans the dead of a battlefield.
photos.k: Why do you think the public was shocked by this photograph?

photos.why: A baby sleeps in a mother's arms in this early color photograph by the British amateur Henry Essenhigh Corke. The warm reds and browns come from the tiny dyed grains in an Autochrome plate.
photos.k: What would it feel like to hold a sleeping baby?

photos.t: A Log Cabin in the Forest
photos.why: Prokudin-Gorsky photographed a small log hut in a green clearing in Russia in color. The grass and trees look as bright and fresh as they would in a modern snapshot.
photos.k: Who might live in a hut like this?

photos.why: The Titanic, the largest ship in the world, left Southampton, England, on April 10, 1912, on her first voyage. She sank four days later after hitting an iceberg, and about 1,500 people lost their lives.
photos.k: How do you think the people on shore felt as she left?

photos.why: Ezra Pound was an American poet who lived in London and helped many other writers get their start. Alvin Langdon Coburn photographed him with a dramatic, intense look.
photos.k: What kind of poetry do you think he wrote?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A boy crouches beside a cow, milking it by hand. Lewis Hine photographed farm children too, since many worked from early morning with their families, long before school.
photos.k: What chores do you have each day?

photos.why: A bright orange bull statue with flower garlands stands near a Hindu temple in Varanasi, India. Banker Albert Kahn sent photographers around the world with color Autochrome plates for his Archives of the Planet, and Stéphane Passet took this one.
photos.k: How old do you think the statue is?

photos.why: A path lined with tall cypress trees leads toward the Taj Mahal in India. This early color picture shows the white marble tomb glowing pink in the light.
photos.k: Where does the path seem to lead?

photos.why: Stéphane Passet photographed Paris in color just before the First World War. The tall buildings and empty street look blue in the early light.
photos.k: Why do you think the street is empty?

photos.why: A shop in Paris with bright red and gold paint, photographed in color in 1914. Early Autochromes captured the colors of ordinary streets before they changed.
photos.k: What would you buy at a shop like this?

photos.why: From the back window of his New York gallery, Alfred Stieglitz photographed a snow-covered tree and the buildings beyond. He made many pictures of the same view in different seasons.
photos.k: Choose a window at home. What would it look like in different seasons?

photos.cr: Gift of Arielle Kozloff Brodkey in memory of Dr. Jerald S. Brodkey
photos.why: Eugène Atget photographed the park at Saint-Cloud, outside Paris, at dawn when it was empty. Two great trees stand over a still pool that doubles them.
photos.k: What do you notice about the water?

photos.why: Frank Hurley was the photographer on Ernest Shackleton's Antarctic expedition. The ship Endurance sits frozen in sea ice under a pink sky, in an image Hurley colored by hand.
photos.k: How would you feel stuck in the ice?

photos.why: Paul Strand photographed small figures hurrying past the huge dark windows of a bank on Wall Street in New York. He made the people look tiny and the building look like a wall, and it became a landmark of modern photography.
photos.k: How do the huge windows make the people feel?

photos.why: Hurley lit the ship Endurance with flashbulbs at night, with the rigging coated in frost. Soon after, the ice crushed the ship, but all twenty-eight men survived by dragging lifeboats across the ice.
photos.k: What would you pack if you had to leave a ship in the ice?

photos.why: Flower sellers and shoppers fill the great square of Kraków in this Autochrome by Tadeusz Rząca. Autochromes made on glass look like stained glass, glowing with color.
photos.k: What do you think the people are buying?

photos.why: San Francisco held a huge world's fair in 1915 to celebrate the opening of the Panama Canal. Arnold Genthe photographed its colonnades and domes in color.
photos.k: What would you want to see at a world's fair?

photos.why: Vegetables, oranges and a jug sit on a table, glowing like stained glass. Autochrome was made on glass plates, and the colors have lasted more than a century.
photos.k: Which food do you want to eat?

photos.why: In 1917 the artist Marcel Duchamp sent a porcelain bathroom fixture, signed R. Mutt, to an art show. The judges refused to show it, so Alfred Stieglitz photographed it in his gallery. The original is lost, and this photograph is the best record of one of the most argued-about artworks ever.
photos.k: Is it art if an artist says it is? What do you think?

photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed the painter Georgia O'Keeffe more than three hundred times over several years. He made close-ups of her face, hands and clothing, as one long portrait.
photos.k: What do her hands tell you about her?

photos.t: Aerial View of the Ruins of Vaux, France
photos.why: Edward Steichen led aerial photography for the US Army in the First World War. His camera in an airplane showed shell craters and ruined villages that the army needed to understand.
photos.k: What can you tell about a battlefield from above?

photos.why: O'Keeffe lifts her hands near her face against a dark background. Stieglitz believed a portrait could be made of a person's hands as well as their face.
photos.k: What do your hands say about you?

photos.why: A colorful Autochrome frames a green garden through a stone arch at an estate near Philadelphia. The color picture shows lawn, trees and flowers in soft greens and pinks.
photos.k: What would you like to do in a garden like this?

photos.why: French soldiers stand in formation near the clock tower in Beirut, a year after the First World War. Frédéric Gadmer took the picture in color for Albert Kahn's Archives of the Planet, an effort to record the world on color plates.
photos.k: Why would someone want to preserve a picture of a regiment?

photos.why: A faint rainbow arches above the hills at Lake George, New York. Stieglitz photographed clouds, trees and skies near his family's summer home, and wanted these images to show feelings as well as places.
photos.k: How is a rainbow different from other things you photograph?

photos.why: Arnold Genthe photographed the old buildings of New Orleans's French Quarter in 1920. The arched doorway and iron lamp belong to a bar that was once famous.
photos.k: What stories could this door tell?

photos.why: Babe Ruth was the best-known baseball player in America. In 1920 he hit 54 home runs for the New York Yankees, a record that amazed fans. Here he poses in his uniform in a studio.
photos.k: How many home runs do you think a player can hit in a season now?

photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed the Paris studio of the sculptor Constantin Brancusi, with its smooth, shining pieces. Brancusi simplified shapes until they seemed to be pure forms.
photos.k: Which sculpture looks like a bird to you?

photos.why: Arnold Genthe photographed dancers in motion in the 1910s and 20s. In this color Autochrome a dancer in flowing blue and yellow fabric leaps in the dark.
photos.k: How does the dancer's cloth help show movement?

photos.why: A worker leans into a huge machine to adjust a bolt with his wrench. Lewis Hine photographed laborers as heroes, to show the skill and strength needed to run modern factories.
photos.k: What do you think he is fixing?

photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed his mother Hedwig, in a rocking chair at the family's Lake George house. The deep lines of her face tell a long story.
photos.k: What might she be thinking about?

photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed the dancer Isadora Duncan performing among the columns of the Parthenon in Athens. She is a tiny figure in the huge, shadowy temple. Duncan danced barefoot in flowing robes and helped invent modern dance.
photos.k: How do the huge columns make the dancer seem?

photos.why: Tree branches swirl against the sky like dancers in a picture made at Lake George. Alfred Stieglitz loved to find shapes and rhythms in nature.
photos.k: What shapes do you see in the branches?

photos.t: Music: A Sequence of Ten Cloud Photographs
photos.why: Stieglitz photographed clouds because critics said his portraits were successful only because of his famous sitters. He wanted to show that a picture of only sky and clouds could make people feel emotions like music does.
photos.k: What kind of music would this sky play?

photos.why: Thomas Edison invented the practical electric light bulb, the phonograph and a movie camera, among over a thousand patents. In this portrait he sits calmly, in his seventies.
photos.k: What would you invent?

photos.t: First Snow and the Little House
photos.why: A small house stands in the snow at Lake George, New York. Stieglitz photographed the same estate for years, in all seasons, making simple scenes feel quiet and personal.
photos.k: What would you do in the first snowfall?

photos.why: Leonora Hughes was an American dancer who became famous in Paris in the 1920s. Edward Steichen photographed her with a cloche hat and pearls, the style of the time.
photos.k: What do you notice about the fashion?

photos.cr: Acquired through exchange with George Eastman House
photos.why: A mother sits near a window holding her baby, in a plain room. Lewis Hine photographed families in need for relief organizations, so people would see who they were helping.
photos.k: What would you give this family?

photos.cr: The Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
photos.why: Eugène Atget photographed a misty park near Paris in early spring. The bare trees and dim light make it feel like a quiet dream.
photos.k: What time of day do you think it is?

photos.t: A Girl in Swedish Folk Costume
photos.why: A young girl wears a white cap and a bright red, yellow and blue costume with braids. This early color photograph preserves the vivid colors of Swedish folk dress.
photos.k: Which colors in the costume stand out the most?

photos.why: In 1925 leaders from several European countries met in Locarno, Switzerland, to agree on treaties to keep peace after the First World War. This color Autochrome shows the delegation from Czechoslovakia.
photos.k: Why do you think countries have such meetings?

photos.why: In 1925 Paris held a huge fair of modern design, the exhibition that gave the Art Deco style its name. The Polish pavilion shows the clean lines and decoration that fair made famous.
photos.k: What shapes do you notice in the pavilion?

photos.why: Two dance partners pose close together in a dramatic embrace. Edward Steichen photographed celebrities for Vanity Fair and Vogue, and made dance look romantic and daring.
photos.k: What dance do you think they are performing?

photos.t: Still Life with Lemons and a Siphon
photos.why: Emmanuel Sougez photographed lemons, a blue soda siphon and printed paper on a table. In the 1920s, photographers began to see ordinary objects as pure shapes and colors.
photos.k: What shapes can you find in the arrangement?

photos.why: Eugène Atget photographed a hairdresser's window in Paris full of mannequin heads in wigs. The Surrealist artists loved this picture because it looks strange and dreamlike.
photos.k: Why does a window full of heads feel odd?

photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz and Georgia O'Keeffe lived high in the Shelton Hotel in New York. From their window, Stieglitz photographed the growing skyscrapers and factory chimneys beyond.
photos.k: What would it be like to look out over the city from so high?

photos.why: Bảo Đại became the emperor of Annam, in what is now Vietnam, as a boy. This color portrait shows him in a dark outfit and cap, as a teenager preparing to rule.
photos.k: What would it be like to be an emperor as a teenager?

photos.why: Paul von Hindenburg was a German general and then president of Germany. This color autochrome from a German magazine shows him in a dark suit with a medal.
photos.k: What do you notice about his face and moustache?

photos.why: Albert Kahn's photographers took color pictures of people all over the world. These two men from the Bahdinan Kurds, in colorful clothes, were photographed on glass plates.
photos.k: Which parts of their clothing do you find most colorful?

photos.why: Edward Steichen became chief photographer for Vogue and Vanity Fair in the 1920s. He photographed this actress in the sleek Art Deco style.
photos.k: How would you pose to look glamorous?

photos.why: Walker Evans was a young photographer in 1929, finding beauty in plain things around him. In this early picture, a woman walks on a boardwalk in a summer dress.
photos.k: What season does it feel like?

photos.t: From My Window at An American Place, North
photos.why: Stieglitz photographed the New York skyline from the window of his gallery. Tall buildings crowd the sky in a hazy gray, as New York grew upward.
photos.k: How many skyscrapers can you count?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Lewis Hine climbed the Empire State Building as it was built to photograph workers high above New York. Here a man works on the mast with a flag as the city spreads out below.
photos.k: Would you be brave enough to work up there?

photos.t: Georgia O'Keeffe: Hands and Horse Skull
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed O'Keeffe's hands as she held a horse skull she had brought back from New Mexico. She painted bones and skulls of the desert as symbols of beauty.
photos.k: Why would a painter love a bone?

photos.t: Climbing Up the Beams on the Empire State Building
photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Lewis Hine climbed the steel frame of the Empire State Building as it rose in 1930 and 1931. He photographed the builders from dizzying angles, showing ordinary workers as heroes.
photos.k: Would you want to work this high above the ground?

photos.why: Skyscrapers, including the shining top of the Chrysler Building, rise above the streets of Manhattan. By 1932 New York had more tall buildings than any other city in the world.
photos.k: Which building do you think is the tallest?

photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed Yellowstone's geysers for a US government project that was supposed to produce murals for the Department of the Interior. The murals were never finished, but his photographs are now in the National Archives.
photos.k: What do you think the steam smells like?

photos.why: Walker Evans photographed the streets of Havana, Cuba, from a rooftop. The picture shows a great square courtyard of apartments and shops, almost like a map.
photos.k: What can you tell about how people lived from this view?

photos.why: Taos Pueblo in New Mexico has multi-story adobe homes where people have lived for about a thousand years. Ansel Adams photographed it under a pale sky for a government project.
photos.k: Why might people build their homes in stacks like this?

photos.t: Schoolchildren Line Up for Free Lunch
photos.why: During the Great Depression many families had little money for food, and schoolchildren lined up for free meals. Photographers recorded these scenes to show how hard times were.
photos.k: How would you feel if you had to line up for lunch like this?

photos.why: Tall chimneys and furnaces rise over the town of Port Pirie, in South Australia, where metals from mines were smelted. Frank Hurley, the explorer-photographer, photographed Australia's industries.
photos.k: What do you think comes out of those chimneys?

photos.why: A bright painted circus poster covers a wall in Alabama. Walker Evans photographed signs and posters across the country as a kind of folk art, and the colors burst through even in black and white.
photos.k: Which performers do you see on the poster?

photos.why: Rows of workers' houses climb the hill under the stacks of a huge steel mill. Walker Evans photographed American towns in the Depression for a government project, and this one is one of his best-known views.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a house in the shadow of a mill?

photos.why: People crowd around a table to collect checks from a government program that helped unemployed workers during the Great Depression. Lewis Hine photographed the New Deal at work.
photos.k: Why would people need help like this?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. James Ward Thorne
photos.why: A studio window in Savannah, Georgia, shows rows of small cheap portraits of local people. Walker Evans loved photographs by ordinary people, and he copied the look of studio displays in his own work.
photos.k: If you could see just one face here, which would you choose?

photos.why: Walker Evans traveled to Alabama with the writer James Agee in 1936 to document the lives of tenant farmers. This small wooden cabin is among the pictures from that trip.
photos.k: What does the cabin look like inside?

photos.why: Allie Mae Burroughs was a young cotton farmer's wife in Alabama, photographed by Walker Evans. She looks straight at the camera with a calm, tired face. The picture is one of the best-known portraits of the Depression.
photos.k: What do you think her life was like?

photos.t: Farmer Walking in a Dust Storm
photos.why: A farmer crosses his yard in Cimarron County, Oklahoma, as a dust storm blows. In the 1930s, drought and wind turned the Great Plains into a Dust Bowl. Arthur Rothstein photographed the storms for the government.
photos.k: What would happen to a crop in a dust storm?

photos.why: In March 1936, Dorothea Lange stopped at a camp of pea pickers in California and photographed a woman named Florence Owens Thompson with her children. The photograph went to newspapers, and food was sent to the camp. It became the most famous image of the Great Depression.
photos.k: What do you see in the mother's face?

photos.why: Two children crouch in the street playing a game, as photographed by Russell Lee. He photographed small-town life across the US for a government project during the Depression.
photos.k: What kind of game do you think they were playing?

photos.why: Shelves of tin cans, flour sacks and cloth fill a country store in Alabama. Walker Evans photographed the things people used every day, as a record of a time.
photos.k: What can you find to buy in this store?

photos.why: Jagged peaks rise above a barren slope in California's Sierra Nevada. Ansel Adams photographed this region in 1936 for the Sierra Club, whose campaign helped to create Kings Canyon National Park.
photos.k: How would you climb up those peaks?

photos.why: Bud Fields was a cotton farmer in Hale County, Alabama. Walker Evans photographed him and his family for the book Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, to show the dignity of people living through hard times.
photos.k: What can you see in his face?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed New York for years to record how fast it was changing. She looked down on this canyon of skyscrapers in the Financial District from above, so the buildings tower and cross like angled walls.
photos.k: How does the high viewpoint make the buildings look?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A wall of dust blows over a farm in Oklahoma in 1936. Dust storms like this carried topsoil hundreds of miles and forced many families to leave their farms.
photos.k: How would you protect a house from dust?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Drifts of dust bury fences and cover a farm. After years without rain, the soil blew away, leaving farmers with nothing to grow.
photos.k: How would you clean up after a storm like this?

photos.why: Hands guide stockings through a machine in a factory. Lewis Hine photographed workers' hands and skills to show that modern industry depended on the people who ran the machines.
photos.k: What do you notice about the hands in this picture?

photos.t: Broke, Baby Sick, and Car Trouble!
photos.why: Dorothea Lange wrote down what people told her, and this family's own words became her title. Their car, loaded with belongings, broke down on a California highway as they searched for work during the Depression.
photos.k: What would you do if your car broke down far from home?

photos.why: On May 6, 1937, the German airship Hindenburg burst into flames as it landed in Lakehurst, New Jersey, killing 36 people. Photographers like Sam Shere were waiting for the landing, and these pictures ended the age of giant passenger airships.
photos.k: Why do you think airships don't carry passengers today?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed New York for years to record how fast it was changing. This hardware store spills pails, paints and tools onto the sidewalk and shows how a shop looked in the 1930s.
photos.k: What tools do you recognize?

photos.why: A barber trims a customer's hair on a porch in a Mississippi town while other men wait. Marion Post Wolcott photographed daily life in the Deep South for the government.
photos.k: Would you want a haircut outdoors?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Pie Town got its name from a woman who baked pies for travelers. Russell Lee photographed its homesteader families in color in 1940, and the pictures give a vivid look at a farming community. Here people gather outside a log church.
photos.k: What does the church building look like?

photos.t: Working on a Vengeance Dive Bomber
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: During World War II, millions of women took jobs in factories. Alfred Palmer photographed women at the Vultee plant in Tennessee as they worked on a dive bomber. His color pictures were meant to show Americans pulling together.
photos.k: What jobs do you think the women are doing?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A woman operates a drilling machine in a factory making airplanes during World War II. Women like her took jobs that men had left to go to war, and posters called them Rosie the Riveter.
photos.k: What would you build if you worked in a factory?

photos.why: Smoking stacks and giant furnaces fill the sky at a steel mill in Maryland. John Vachon photographed American towns and factories for the Farm Security Administration.
photos.k: What do you think steel was used for?

photos.why: John Vachon photographed the tall buildings of Chicago's Michigan Avenue from a street corner. Chicago invented the skyscraper, and this street shows why people loved the city.
photos.k: How many tall buildings can you count?

photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed children in the American South on color film. At a time when most photographs were black-and-white, her color pictures show warm clothing and sunlight.
photos.k: What color do you notice first?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Four girls smile in a classroom in a small New Mexico town. Russell Lee photographed their one-room school and the children who came from farms for miles around.
photos.k: What would it be like to go to a one-room school?

photos.why: A tank kicks up a cloud of dust under a bright blue sky in this color photograph from 1942. Alfred Palmer photographed tanks being tested at an arsenal in Michigan, where factories that once built cars built weapons for World War II.
photos.k: What do you hear when a tank roars past?

photos.why: A street corner shop with a bright awning, ads and an old car outside, photographed in color in 1942. Most photos from this time are black-and-white, so color shows how lively ordinary streets were.
photos.k: What would you buy at a fruit store like this?

photos.t: The Tetons and the Snake River
photos.why: The Snake River curls through a valley below the jagged Teton Range in Wyoming. Ansel Adams's picture is one of the most famous landscapes ever made. It was even included on the Voyager spacecraft's Golden Record, sent out into the solar system.
photos.k: If aliens saw this picture, what would they think?

photos.why: Gordon Parks, then a young photographer, photographed Ella Watson, a cleaning woman, standing in front of an American flag with a mop and broom. He named it after a famous painting, and it was a quiet protest against racism in the nation's capital.
photos.k: What do you think Ella Watson would say about her life?

photos.why: A young girl holds a box camera and takes a photograph in Washington, D.C. Esther Bubley photographed ordinary American life, including children and their hobbies.
photos.k: What would you photograph if you held a camera like this?

photos.t: U.S. Ships Under Attack Off Kwajalein
photos.why: Dark puffs of exploding shells fill the sky over a fleet of ships off Kwajalein in the Pacific. Edward Steichen, famous for art photographs, led the US Navy photography unit in World War II.
photos.k: What can a photograph show that a report can't?

photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed the great jazz bandleader Duke Ellington at a table with friends in a lively club. Parks became the first Black photographer on the staff of Life magazine.
photos.k: What kind of music do you imagine they were listening to?

photos.t: Times Square on a Rainy Day
photos.why: The rain makes the pavement shine at Times Square in New York. John Vachon photographed the glittering signs and umbrellas during the war.
photos.k: What colors would the neon signs be?

photos.why: During World War II, the US government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes into camps like Manzanar in California. Ansel Adams photographed daily life there, including young people stretching in the morning.
photos.k: Why do you think it is important to remember what happened?

photos.why: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Tehran, Iran, in 1943 to plan how to win the war. The photograph of the three sitting together became famous around the world.
photos.k: What do you think they are talking about?

photos.t: Duke Ellington at the Hurricane Ballroom
photos.why: A saxophone player performs under the lights at New York's Hurricane Ballroom. Duke Ellington's orchestra was one of the greatest in jazz.
photos.k: How would you play a saxophone?

photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a Chicago rail yard in color, with the Wrigley Building and other skyscrapers in the background. Trains moved the soldiers, food and goods that powered the war effort.
photos.k: What do the trains carry?

photos.why: A woman kneels to place flowers on a soldier's grave at Arlington National Cemetery on Memorial Day. White stones stretch into the distance, and a war was still going on. Esther Bubley photographed it for the Office of War Information.
photos.k: Who do you think she is remembering?

photos.why: On June 6, 1944, D-Day, Allied soldiers waded ashore at Omaha Beach in Normandy, France, under heavy fire. Coast Guard photographer Robert Sargent took this picture of troops leaving their landing craft, and it became one of the best-known pictures of the invasion.
photos.k: What would you be thinking as you stepped off the boat?

photos.t: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima
photos.why: On February 23, 1945, six US Marines raised the American flag on top of Mount Suribachi during the battle of Iwo Jima. Joe Rosenthal's photograph won the Pulitzer Prize and became the model for a famous memorial.
photos.k: How does the diagonal line of the flagpole make the picture feel?

photos.why: In May 1945, American troops liberated Ebensee, a Nazi concentration camp in Austria. The survivors in this photograph stare at the camera. Pictures like this showed the world what had happened and are kept as evidence so it is never forgotten.
photos.k: Why is it important to remember difficult history?

photos.why: On August 14, 1945, news of Japan's surrender set off wild celebrations in Times Square. In this picture by the US Navy photographer Victor Jorgensen, a sailor kisses a nurse, a joyful moment at the end of World War II.
photos.k: What do you see in the crowd that shows how people felt?

photos.why: Senator John F. Kennedy married Jacqueline Bouvier in Newport, Rhode Island, in September 1953. The photographer Toni Frissell captured the new couple leaving the church. Kennedy became president in 1961.
photos.k: What do you notice about the wedding dress?

photos.why: In 1947 Jackie Robinson became the first Black player in modern major-league baseball, when he joined the Brooklyn Dodgers. He faced insults and threats, and won the first Rookie of the Year award. Here he stands with his bat, number 42, which every team has since retired.
photos.k: What does it take to be the first at something?

photos.why: At seventy-five, the photographer Imogen Cunningham photographed her own reflection in a shop window in San Francisco, through the glass, with her camera held at her waist. She made art until she was in her nineties.
photos.k: How many ways can you find yourself in a reflection?

photos.why: Neil Armstrong flew the X-15 rocket plane, which could reach the edge of space, before he flew Apollo. He stands beside it in his pressure suit. Nine years later, he became the first person to walk on the Moon.
photos.k: What would it be like to fly to the edge of space?

photos.why: On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, orbiting Earth in a spacecraft called Vostok 1 for 108 minutes. This portrait shows him with his famous broad smile.
photos.k: What would you say if you were the first person in space?

photos.why: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people marched to the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., to demand jobs and freedom for all Americans. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his "I Have a Dream" speech that day. Here marchers, including King, walk together.
photos.k: What would you have carried on a sign?

photos.why: On Christmas Eve 1968, astronaut William Anders photographed Earth rising above the Moon's horizon from Apollo 8. It was the first time people saw the whole Earth from deep space, a small, blue, fragile marble. The picture helped inspire the environmental movement.
photos.k: What does it feel like to see our whole planet from far away?

photos.t: Neil Armstrong in the Lunar Module
photos.why: After the first moonwalk, Neil Armstrong sits in the lunar module with moon dust on his suit. There are almost no pictures of Armstrong on the Moon because he carried the camera. Buzz Aldrin took this one.
photos.k: Why are there so few pictures of the first man on the Moon?

photos.why: Buzz Aldrin photographed his bootprint in the lunar soil to study how fine and powdery the dust was. Because there is no wind or rain on the Moon, the print could last for millions of years.
photos.k: What would leave a footprint on the Moon for millions of years?

photos.why: Neil Armstrong photographed Buzz Aldrin saluting the US flag on the Moon in July 1969. The flag has a stiff rod along the top so it seems to wave in a place with no air.
photos.k: Why did they need a rod to hold the flag out?

photos.why: Buzz Aldrin stands in his white suit on the gray lunar plain. In his gold visor you can see a reflection of Neil Armstrong, the photographer, and the lunar module Eagle.
photos.k: Can you find Armstrong in the reflection?

photos.why: On December 7, 1972, the crew of Apollo 17, flying to the Moon, photographed the whole Earth in sunlight from about 29,000 kilometers away. It became one of the most widely printed photographs in history.
photos.k: Where do you think you live on this ball?

photos.why: From 1971 to 1977, the US Environmental Protection Agency hired photographers in a project called Documerica to record how Americans lived and what the environment looked like. Here a logger, or faller, works on a giant red fir in the Pacific Northwest.
photos.k: How do you think trees are cut down safely?

photos.why: Apollo 17 was the last time people walked on the Moon. The astronauts used a battery-powered Lunar Roving Vehicle, a "moon buggy," to explore far from the lander at about 11 miles an hour.
photos.k: What would you want to find on the Moon?

photos.why: Empty wooden buildings stand in a town in the West where the gold and silver ran out and the people left. This color photograph is part of the EPA's Documerica project of the early 1970s.
photos.k: What stories could these empty buildings tell?

photos.why: Cotton grass, which isn't really cotton, grows in the marshes of Alaska, with white tufts like puffs of cotton. The photographer Dennis Cowals recorded it for the Documerica project.
photos.k: What do you think the tufts are for?

photos.t: Maid of the Mist, Niagara Falls
photos.why: A sightseeing boat carries visitors close to the mist of Niagara Falls. Boats have taken tourists into the spray since the 1840s.
photos.k: Would you get wet on this ride?

photos.why: In 1973, an oil shortage meant many gas stations ran out of fuel, and signs like this appeared across America. Photographers for the EPA's Documerica project recorded how the energy crisis changed daily life.
photos.k: What would you do if there were no gas for the car?

photos.why: In July 1975 an American Apollo spacecraft and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked in orbit, and the astronauts and cosmonauts shook hands in space. At the time the two countries were rivals, so the mission was a symbol of cooperation. Here the crews pose together before the flight.
photos.k: Why was it important for rivals to work together in space?

photos.why: Two Voyager spacecraft launched in 1977 each carry a gold-plated record containing greetings in 55 languages, music, and 115 pictures of Earth for any aliens that might find them. The cover shows instructions for playing it.
photos.k: What song would you put on a record for aliens?

photos.why: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system, about three times as tall as Mount Everest. NASA's Viking orbiters photographed it in the 1970s and sent the pictures to Earth.
photos.k: How would you climb a mountain this big?

photos.why: Challenger was the second space shuttle to fly into orbit. Shuttles were rocket-launched like a rocket and landed like airplanes, and they could carry satellites and astronauts into space again and again.
photos.k: What do you think the roaring sound is like?

photos.why: In February 1984, astronaut Bruce McCandless flew freely, without a safety line, away from the space shuttle using a jet-powered backpack. He drifted more than 300 feet away, with Earth far below.
photos.k: Would you be brave enough to float in space like this?

photos.why: On January 28, 1986, the space shuttle Challenger broke apart seventy-three seconds after liftoff. All seven crew members died, including Christa McAuliffe, a teacher who was going to teach lessons from space. The disaster led to major safety changes.
photos.k: What can we learn when something goes wrong?

photos.why: Comet Hale-Bopp was one of the brightest comets in decades, visible to the naked eye for eighteen months in 1996 and 1997. Philipp Salzgeber photographed it above a tree in the evening sky.
photos.k: What would you wish for if you saw a comet?

photos.why: Eleven men eat lunch while sitting on a steel beam hundreds of feet above New York in 1932. The picture, probably staged as publicity for Rockefeller Center, shows the daring of the ironworkers who built the city's skyscrapers.
photos.k: How would you feel sitting on that beam?

photos.why: The calm eye of Hurricane Isabel is surrounded by thick spiraling clouds. Astronaut Ed Lu photographed it from the International Space Station, about 250 miles above Earth.
photos.k: Why do you think the eye of a hurricane is calm?

photos.why: Hubble stared at one tiny dark patch of sky for many days and found about ten thousand galaxies. The patch is so small that it would look like a grain of sand held at arm's length. Each dot is a whole galaxy with billions of stars.
photos.k: What do you think this says about how big the universe is?

photos.why: These towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula are a place where new stars are being born. The tallest pillar is about four light-years long. Hubble's picture, taken in 1995, became one of the most famous space photographs.
photos.k: How long would it take to travel four light-years?

photos.why: The Andromeda Galaxy is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away. This view, taken in ultraviolet light, shows its spiral arms glowing blue and white.
photos.k: Which arm of the spiral would you want to visit?

photos.t: Clouds Over the Caldera, La Palma
photos.why: Clouds spill over the rim of a huge volcanic crater on La Palma, one of the Canary Islands. The pines on the slope are green and thick above the sea of cloud.
photos.k: What do you think it feels like to walk through a cloud?

photos.why: On December 26, 2004, an undersea earthquake sent giant waves across the Indian Ocean, killing more than 200,000 people in fourteen countries. This picture was taken at a beach resort as the first big wave arrived, when most people did not yet understand what was coming.
photos.k: Why is it important to have tsunami warning systems?

photos.why: This spiral galaxy, about 12 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major, glows with billions of stars. Hubble's picture shows the bright core and the dark lanes of dust that curl around it.
photos.k: What do the dark lanes look like to you?

photos.why: This dark, towering shape in the Eagle Nebula is a pillar of gas and dust where new stars are forming. Hubble photographed it and scientists nicknamed it the Fairy.
photos.k: Do you see why they call it a fairy?

photos.why: Ribbons of green and purple light dance over a snowy field near Eielson Air Force Base in Alaska. Auroras happen when particles from the Sun hit Earth's upper atmosphere.
photos.k: What color would you paint the sky?

photos.why: At the U.S. Naval Academy, graduating midshipmen toss their white caps into the air at the end of the ceremony. It is a tradition that has become a joyful snapshot of celebration.
photos.k: Can you spot a cap in mid-air?

photos.why: The Crab Nebula is the glowing leftover of a star that exploded in the year 1054, which astronomers in China recorded. This picture combines many Hubble Space Telescope images into one.
photos.k: How do you think a star explosion could light up space for a thousand years?

photos.why: Huge waves smash into small fishing boats on the coast of Brittany, in France. Photographer Henri Camus captured the moment the sea blew spray high into the air.
photos.k: What would you do if you were on the shore in a storm?

photos.why: Two babies in woolly winter hats lean in for a kiss. The photograph by Yogi was shared freely on Wikimedia Commons and was chosen as a Featured Picture.
photos.k: What do you think each baby is thinking?

photos.why: Thousands of king penguins stand together on a green hillside above the sea, with chicks in brown fluff among the adults. They live on islands in the cold southern ocean.
photos.k: Can you find a fluffy chick?

photos.why: An elderly holy man called a baba, or sadhu, in Nepal wears a coiled turban and has a long white beard. Wen-Yan King photographed his deeply lined face and bright colors.
photos.k: What can you tell about his life from his face?

photos.why: Boats float along a canal lined with tall, narrow brick houses in Amsterdam, in the Netherlands. The city's ring of canals was dug in the 1600s and is now a World Heritage Site.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a house on a canal?

photos.t: A Tibetan Woman with a Prayer Wheel
photos.why: An elderly Tibetan woman holds a prayer wheel, a spinning cylinder with prayers inside. Luca Galuzzi photographed her in a street in a bright, patterned coat.
photos.k: What would you put inside a prayer wheel?

photos.why: A male gadwall, a kind of duck, floats on blue water with its feathers in fine gray and brown patterns. Close-up photographs show details you may never notice when a duck swims by.
photos.k: How many different patterns can you count?
