photos.why: A bright old car is parked on a cobbled street in Trinidad, a Cuban town full of colorful colonial buildings. The town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
photos.k: Which color house is your favorite?

photos.why: A red train winds through deep snow on the Bernina Railway in the Swiss Alps. The line, which climbs through mountains and over high viaducts, is a World Heritage Site.
photos.k: Would you like to ride on this train?

photos.why: The Aletsch Glacier, in the Swiss Alps, is the longest glacier in the Alps, at about 23 kilometers. Rivers of ice flow down between the mountains in the photograph.
photos.k: What do you think a glacier feels like?

photos.why: A slim blue damselfly rests on a leaf in Osaka, Japan. Its wings are as clear as glass and its eyes are huge compared to its tiny body.
photos.k: How is a damselfly different from a dragonfly?

photos.why: A red train crosses a tall curved stone viaduct high above a Swiss gorge. The Landwasser Viaduct was built in 1902 and is part of a railway that is now a World Heritage Site.
photos.k: How would you feel crossing a bridge this high?

photos.why: Gray beech trees stand in winter light in the Mátra Mountains of Hungary, with a few leaves still clinging. The quiet forest looks almost like a painting.
photos.k: What sounds do you hear in a winter forest?

photos.why: Air Force special tactics airmen leap from an airplane over the ocean. Military photographers shoot training missions like this one.
photos.k: How would you feel stepping out of a plane?

photos.why: A tall baobab stands in Madagascar, with a giant, smooth trunk and a tuft of branches on top. Baobabs store water in their trunks and can live for centuries.
photos.k: Why does the tree look as if it is upside down?

photos.why: NASA made this view of Earth by putting together many satellite images into one sphere. Clouds, oceans and continents appear as if seen from space.
photos.k: Can you find North and South America?

photos.why: A mountain vizcacha, a rabbit-like rodent related to chinchillas, sits on a rock in Bolivia's highlands. It lives in rocky areas and has a soft coat to keep warm.
photos.k: What does it remind you of?

photos.why: A row of red dots shows the Moon passing in front of the Sun during the eclipse of August 1, 2008. The photographer used the same camera, in one place, to record each stage.
photos.k: What would you see if you looked at the Sun? (Never do this without special glasses!)

photos.why: Giant granite boulders and palms frame a pale sandy beach on La Digue, in the Seychelles. The boulders are billions of years old.
photos.k: What would you do first on this beach?

photos.why: NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft flew past Mercury in 2008 and took color pictures. The colors have been exaggerated so scientists can see differences in the rock and dust.
photos.k: Why would scientists change the colors in a photograph?

photos.why: A little wattlebird, an Australian honeyeater, perches among bright red flowers. Its long, curved bill is perfect for sipping nectar.
photos.k: What does the bird eat?

photos.t: The Golden Gate Bridge from Baker Beach
photos.why: The Golden Gate Bridge, painted "International Orange," spans the entrance to San Francisco Bay. When it opened in 1937 it was the longest suspension bridge in the world.
photos.k: Why do you think they chose orange?

photos.why: A macro photograph of a blowfly's face shows its huge compound eyes, made of thousands of tiny lenses, and the bristly hairs on its head. J. J. Harrison made the picture by combining many photos taken at different focus depths.
photos.k: How do you think a fly sees the world?

photos.why: Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is the highest mountain on Earth, at nearly 8,850 meters. Clouds blow like a banner from its summit.
photos.k: Would you want to climb it?

photos.why: An American toad sits on a rock with golden eyes and bumpy skin. It eats insects, slugs and spiders, and sings in a long trill.
photos.k: What do you notice about its eyes?

photos.by: Alchemist-hp + Richard Bartz with focus stack
photos.why: This stair-stepped crystal was grown from the element bismuth. A thin layer of oxide on its surface makes the rainbow colors, like oil on water. The crystals grow in square spirals.
photos.k: How is it like a staircase?

photos.why: The Carina Nebula is a huge cloud of gas and dust about 7,500 light-years away where many new stars are being born. This image comes from the European Southern Observatory's telescopes in Chile.
photos.k: What do the colors and shapes remind you of?

photos.why: The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American military pilots in the US, trained in Alabama. They flew thousands of missions in World War II. Toni Frissell photographed one of them in Italy in 1945.
photos.k: Why was it important for the Tuskegee Airmen to prove themselves?

photos.why: The Inca built the city of Machu Picchu high in the Andes mountains of Peru, around 1450. Its stone walls and terraces fit perfectly without mortar, and clouds often drift between the peaks.
photos.k: How do you think people carried stone up here?

photos.t: Wreck of the Gratitude, Macquarie Island
photos.why: Frank Hurley was the photographer on Douglas Mawson's expedition to Antarctica in 1911. On the way he photographed the wreck of the ship Gratitude and hundreds of penguins on Macquarie Island, a stop between Australia and the ice.
photos.k: How many penguins can you count?

photos.why: Bright orange and golden autumn colors cover a valley in northern Norway, with snowy peaks in the distance. The photographer Simo Räsänen captured it in the soft light of fall.
photos.k: What do you like best about autumn?

photos.why: A sharp mountain rises behind a blue mountain lake in the Pyrenees, on the border of France and Spain. Its two points make it one of the most recognizable peaks in the range.
photos.k: Where would you put your picnic?

photos.why: Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland, photographed two children playing a board game of draughts, which Americans call checkers. He made many photographs of children, which he took in the garden or in his rooms at Oxford.
photos.k: Which child do you think is winning?

photos.why: The grey crowned crane has a golden crown of stiff feathers and a red cheek patch. It lives in the grasslands of Africa, and is Uganda's national bird.
photos.k: What do you think the crown is for?

photos.why: The Aqueduct of Segovia in Spain was built about 2,000 years ago by the Romans to carry water from the mountains into the city. Its 167 arches are made of granite blocks stacked without mortar.
photos.k: How could stones stay up without glue?

photos.why: A hot-air balloon is inflated with a rainbow of colors. Cappadocia in Turkey is famous for balloon rides at sunrise over its fairy-chimney rocks.
photos.k: Which color would you like on your balloon?

photos.why: This brown, many-sided crystal is a kind of garnet called andradite. Its natural flat faces form without anyone cutting them, as atoms line up as it grows.
photos.k: How can a rock grow flat faces by itself?

photos.why: In January 2010, a satellite photographed Great Britain covered in snow, with clouds drifting over the North Sea. The picture shows the whole island at once.
photos.k: Can you find your country on a map? What would it look like from space?

photos.why: This wooden box camera was made by Susse Frères in 1839, the year Daguerre's photographic process was announced to the world. It has a brass lens in front and a place for the silver plate at the back.
photos.k: How is it different from a camera today?

photos.t: Space Shuttle Endeavour on the Launch Pad
photos.why: The space shuttle Endeavour stands on its launch pad, attached to its orange fuel tank and two white boosters. It was one of the last shuttles to fly before the program ended in 2011.
photos.k: What do you think the launch sounds like?

photos.why: A castle with turrets stands among autumn trees beside a still lake, mirrored in the water. Svirzh Castle is in western Ukraine.
photos.k: Would you like to live in a castle?

photos.why: The emperor dragonfly is one of the largest dragonflies in Europe. It hunts other insects in flight, and its wings are as clear as glass.
photos.k: How fast do you think it can fly?

photos.t: The Last Shuttle at the Space Station
photos.why: In July 2011, a Soyuz spacecraft flew around the International Space Station with the space shuttle Atlantis attached, and photographed it. It was the last flight of the shuttle program, and this is the only photograph of a shuttle docked at the station from the outside, from a Soyuz.
photos.k: What do you think the astronauts felt when the shuttle program ended?

photos.t: Charles Lindbergh and the Spirit of St. Louis
photos.why: In May 1927, Charles Lindbergh flew alone, without stopping, from New York to Paris in a small plane called the Spirit of St. Louis. The flight took thirty-three and a half hours and made him the most famous person in the world.
photos.k: How would you stay awake for thirty-three hours?

photos.why: A shaggy yak stands in front of the snowy Annapurna mountains in Nepal. Yaks live at high altitudes and carry loads for people trekking in the Himalayas.
photos.k: How do you think its thick coat helps?

photos.why: NASA's Mars rover Curiosity took a selfie by combining dozens of photographs from the camera at the end of its robot arm. The arm doesn't show, so the rover seems to float in its sandy landscape.
photos.k: What would you tell the rover to do next?

photos.why: Tall pillars of sandstone covered with trees rise out of mist in Zhangjiajie, in Hunan, China. The strange landscape inspired the floating mountains in the movie Avatar.
photos.k: What do the pillars remind you of?

photos.by: This Photo was taken by Wolfgang Moroder
photos.why: A gondola glides along the Grand Canal in Venice, with the domes of the church of Santa Maria della Salute behind. The city was built on islands in a lagoon, and boats are its streets.
photos.k: What would you do in a city with no cars?

photos.why: The golden columns of a Greek temple stand on a ridge above the sea in Agrigento, Sicily. Greek settlers built the temples about 2,450 years ago, and many of the columns are still standing.
photos.k: How do you think they lifted such big stones?

photos.why: The Sombrero Galaxy, about 28 million light-years away, looks like a wide-brimmed hat. In this view from NASA's Spitzer telescope, which sees infrared light, its ring of dust glows.
photos.k: Why do you think astronomers named it after a hat?

photos.why: Worshippers throw yellow turmeric powder in the air at a festival at a hilltop temple in Maharashtra, India. The powder turns the whole scene golden.
photos.k: What color would you choose for a festival?

photos.why: The Parthenon crowns the rocky hill of the Acropolis in Athens. It was built about 2,450 years ago to honor the goddess Athena, and the city has grown around it.
photos.k: What do you think Athens looked like when the Parthenon was new?

photos.why: Fishermen pull a boat through the surf, with waves crashing around them. In many places around the world, people still fish from small boats and haul them ashore by hand.
photos.k: How hard do you think this work is?

photos.why: A school of yellow-and-blue fish swims together in the clear water off Fiji. Fish swim in groups to confuse predators, and they all turn as if they were one animal.
photos.k: Why does swimming in a group protect them?

photos.why: This wooden church in Norway was built about 1180 and has dragon heads on its roof. Stave churches are made with upright wooden posts, and this is the best preserved one in the country.
photos.k: Why do you think the roof has dragons?

photos.why: Captain Edward Gleed, an Army Air Forces pilot with the Tuskegee Airmen, leans on his P-51 Mustang fighter in Italy in 1945. Toni Frissell photographed him in a sheepskin jacket, with his cap on.
photos.k: What do you think it was like to fly a fighter plane?

photos.why: On August 6, 1945, an atomic bomb exploded almost directly above this building in Hiroshima, Japan. Its shell survived and was preserved as a memorial that reminds people of the need for peace.
photos.k: Why would a city keep a ruin like this?

photos.t: The Bastei Bridge in Morning Light
photos.why: Tall sandstone pillars rise above forests in Saxon Switzerland, in Germany, with a stone bridge from 1851 spanning the gaps between them. Painters and hikers have loved the view for centuries.
photos.k: How would you cross between the rocks without a bridge?

photos.t: An Inupiat Family from Noatak, Alaska
photos.why: Edward Curtis photographed an Inupiat family in thick fur parkas on his trips to Alaska in the late 1920s. A mother and father look at the camera, with a baby peeking out from the furs.
photos.k: How do you think fur keeps people warm in the Arctic?

photos.why: A dancer in a bright orange costume poses in a classical Indian dance called Bharatanatyam. It comes from southern India and uses hand gestures and facial expressions to tell stories.
photos.k: Can you copy her pose?

photos.why: The great dome of Florence's cathedral glows in the evening, across the roofs of the city. Brunelleschi's dome, finished in 1436, was the largest brick dome in the world.
photos.k: How did they build such a huge dome?

photos.why: In 2014, Hubble photographed the Pillars of Creation again with a new camera, giving a sharper, clearer view. The pillars are columns of gas and dust, and the light from them takes thousands of years to reach us.
photos.k: What looks different from the 1995 picture?

photos.why: During the total lunar eclipse of April 15, 2014, the Moon turned deep red. Sunlight bends through Earth's atmosphere to reach the Moon, and only the red light makes it, so sunset colors fall on the Moon.
photos.k: Why would the Moon turn red?

photos.t: The Moon Setting from the Space Station
photos.why: Astronaut Reid Wiseman photographed the Moon setting beyond the curve of Earth's atmosphere. From orbit, the atmosphere is a thin blue line.
photos.k: What does it feel like to see the whole Earth's edge?

photos.why: The bee hummingbird, which lives only in Cuba, is the smallest bird in the world, about 5 centimeters long and weighing around two grams. Its wings beat so fast they blur.
photos.k: How do you think such a tiny bird finds enough food?

photos.why: This image of a comet shows the rubbery-looking nucleus of Comet 67P, which the European Space Agency's Rosetta spacecraft studied for two years. On September 30, 2016, Rosetta landed softly on the comet to end its mission.
photos.k: What does a comet look like up close compared with the pictures of faraway ones?

photos.why: On August 21, 2017, the Moon covered the Sun across the United States. Just as totality ends, a bright spot of sunlight peeks through valleys on the Moon's edge, called the diamond ring effect. NASA photographer Carla Thomas captured it.
photos.k: Why are special glasses needed to look at a partial eclipse?

photos.why: NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory watches the Sun all day and night in many colors of ultraviolet light. Here it shows a big solar flare, a sudden burst of energy that can affect satellites and power grids.
photos.k: How is the Sun different from what we see in the sky?

photos.t: Hurricane Florence from the Space Station
photos.why: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station photographed Hurricane Florence in September 2018 as it grew over the Atlantic. The huge storm has an open eye in the middle, with towering clouds spiraling around.
photos.k: How big do you think a hurricane is compared with a country?

photos.why: Oscar Rejlander photographed a crying child for Charles Darwin's book about emotions. Darwin wanted to show that people everywhere show feelings in the same ways, and photographs helped him prove it.
photos.k: What does your face do when you feel sad?

photos.why: Tall green bamboo stalks fill a path in the Arashiyama forest, near Kyoto in Japan. Some bamboo can grow up to a meter in a single day.
photos.k: What sound do you think the stalks make in the wind?

photos.t: A Golden Eagle in the Alps
photos.why: A golden eagle soars in front of the snowy Alps. Golden eagles are among the largest birds of prey, with a wingspan of up to about two meters, and they can spot small animals from far away.
photos.k: How far do you think an eagle can see?

photos.t: A Marmot in the Swiss Alps
photos.why: A wild alpine marmot sits in the grass in the mountains, watching. Marmots whistle to warn each other of danger and sleep through the winter in deep burrows.
photos.k: What would you whistle to warn a friend?

photos.why: This small bird has bright blue feathers and a long tail with a crest on its head. It lives in the forests of central Africa. Giles Laurent photographed it in Uganda's Kibale National Park.
photos.k: How do you think a long tail helps a bird?

photos.why: An alpha male chimpanzee sits quietly in the forest, looking at the camera. Chimpanzees are one of our closest living relatives and share about 98 percent of our DNA.
photos.k: What do you think he is thinking?

photos.t: The Pillars of Creation, Seen by Webb
photos.why: In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope looked at the Pillars of Creation in near-infrared light, which can see through dust. The red dots at the tips are baby stars just beginning to form.
photos.k: How is this different from the Hubble pictures of the same pillars?

photos.why: On July 12, 2022, NASA shared Webb's first full-color images. The Cosmic Cliffs are the edge of a huge cloud of gas in the Carina Nebula where stars are forming. The mountains and valleys seem to glow, though the tallest peaks are about seven light-years high.
photos.k: How can gas clouds look like mountains?

photos.why: A dying star at the center has puffed off layers of gas. Webb photographed it in two different kinds of infrared light, on the left with its near-infrared camera and on the right with its mid-infrared one, and the images show different details.
photos.k: Which picture shows more of the central stars?

photos.why: This nudibranch, or sea slug, wears bright blue and purple colors to warn predators that it tastes bad. Many sea slugs get chemicals from the sponges they eat and use them as defense.
photos.k: Why would a snail without a shell have such bright colors?

photos.why: The Roman Bridge crosses the Guadalquivir River in Córdoba, with the city's great cathedral behind it. The cathedral began as a mosque more than a thousand years ago, and still has hundreds of red-and-white arches inside.
photos.k: What would you cross to reach this city?

photos.why: The Andromeda Galaxy can be seen with the naked eye on a dark night, but a long exposure shows its swirling arms. Amateurs now make photographs of galaxies that would have needed observatories in the past.
photos.k: How many stars do you think Andromeda has?

photos.why: Herbert Ponting was the photographer on Captain Scott's Terra Nova expedition to Antarctica. He photographed a member of the team standing in a blue ice cave in an iceberg. Ponting was the first professional photographer to work in Antarctica.
photos.k: How cold do you think it was inside the ice?

photos.t: The Church of St. John at Kaneo
photos.why: A small stone church stands on a cliff above Lake Ohrid, in North Macedonia. It was built in the 1200s, and the water below is among the deepest and oldest lakes in Europe.
photos.k: How do you think people got to the church?

photos.why: A round nest hangs among the leaves of a tree. Stingless bees live in many warm countries, making honey and wax but, as their name says, not stinging.
photos.k: How do you think they build a ball hanging from a branch?

photos.why: Comet C/2022 E3 (ZTF) glows green because its gas contains carbon molecules that shine in sunlight. It passed close to Earth in early 2023, for the first time in about 50,000 years.
photos.k: What do you think will happen to the comet next?

photos.why: A Polynesian flying fox, a kind of fruit bat, spreads its wings against a blue sky. With wings that can span almost a meter, it flies at night to eat fruit and spreads seeds.
photos.k: How is a fruit bat different from a bird?

photos.why: In 1840, the Viennese mathematician Joseph Petzval designed a lens by calculation, making it about twenty times faster than earlier ones. Portrait exposures dropped from minutes to seconds, and Voigtländer made the brass lens in this photograph.
photos.k: Why was a faster lens such a big change for portraits?

photos.why: Earth, a bright crescent of blue, sets behind the horizon of the Moon, photographed from NASA's Orion spacecraft in 2026. Like the Earthrise pictures of Apollo, it shows how our planet looks from the Moon.
photos.k: Which one do you think looks more beautiful, an earthrise or an earthset?

collections.name: Photos for Kids
collections.blurb: Animals, space, firsts and funny faces, with a challenge to find something in each.
collections.intro: These are the photographs kids tend to love: animals up close, rockets and rovers, the very first pictures ever taken, and a few surprises. Each one has a "look closer" challenge.

collections.name: The First Photographs
collections.blurb: Silver plates, paper negatives and the people who were brave enough to sit still.
collections.intro: These pictures were made in the first twenty-five years of photography, between 1826 and 1850, when making a single picture could take hours of sunshine and a lot of chemistry.

collections.name: The American Civil War
collections.blurb: Brady, Gardner, O'Sullivan and Barnard carried cameras to the battlefields.
collections.intro: The Civil War was the first big American war to be photographed. Cameras were too slow to catch the fighting, so photographers recorded camps, ruins and the places where battles had been fought.

collections.name: Photographing the American West
collections.blurb: Watkins, Jackson, O'Sullivan and Adams showed Americans their own wild lands.
collections.intro: Before there were highways and airplanes, photographers hauled huge cameras by mule to Yosemite, Yellowstone and the deserts. Their pictures helped people see why wild places were worth protecting.

collections.name: The Great Depression
collections.blurb: The government sent photographers across America to record hard times.
collections.intro: In the 1930s, a Farm Security Administration photography unit hired Dorothea Lange, Walker Evans and others to record what the Depression and the Dust Bowl did to American families.

collections.name: Color Before Color Film
collections.blurb: Autochromes, photochroms and three-filter color from a century ago.
collections.intro: Color photographs are older than you think. The Lumière brothers' Autochrome plates, Prokudin-Gorsky's three-color process and the Swiss photochrom all gave people glimpses of the world in color long before color film.

collections.name: Women Behind the Camera
collections.blurb: Cameron, Käsebier, Lange, Abbott and more.
collections.intro: Women were making great photographs from the start. Julia Margaret Cameron began at 48, Gertrude Käsebier ran New York's busiest portrait studio, and Dorothea Lange gave the Depression a face.

collections.name: Lewis Hine and the Children of Work
collections.blurb: Photographs that helped change the law.
collections.intro: Between 1908 and 1920 Lewis Hine photographed children working in mills, mines and streets for the National Child Labor Committee. His pictures helped end child labor in the United States.

collections.name: Photography as Art
collections.blurb: Stieglitz, Steichen, Käsebier, White and Coburn argued that photographs could be art.
collections.intro: Around 1900, Alfred Stieglitz and a circle of friends began to insist that photographs could be as beautiful as paintings. They made soft, dreamy pictures, then sharp, modern ones.

collections.name: Paris Through the Lens
collections.blurb: Marville, Atget, Nadar and the streets of the City of Light.
collections.intro: Paris has been photographed since the very beginning. Marville recorded streets before they were torn down, Atget photographed it at dawn, and Nadar took portraits and the first aerial pictures.

collections.name: Egypt and the Nile
collections.blurb: Sphinxes, temples and Nile travelers' cameras.
collections.intro: Photographers have been going to Egypt since the 1840s. Du Camp, Frith and Greene hauled cameras up the Nile to photograph temples that were half buried in sand.

collections.name: Asia Through the Lens
collections.blurb: India, China, Burma and Japan in the 1800s.
collections.intro: Photographers like Felice Beato, Samuel Bourne, John Thomson and Raja Deen Dayal made some of the first photographs of India, China and Southeast Asia.

collections.name: Out of This World
collections.blurb: From the Moon to the edge of the universe.
collections.intro: Cameras went to space almost as soon as people did. These photographs, from the first moonwalk to the Webb Space Telescope, show our planet and the cosmos as no one had seen them before.

collections.name: Animals and Nature
collections.blurb: Birds, bugs, crystals and creatures, up close.
collections.intro: Modern cameras can freeze a hummingbird or show the eye of a fly. These photographs from Wikimedia Commons show wild things in sharp detail.

collections.name: Faces of History
collections.blurb: Lincoln, Douglass, Darwin, Tubman, Edison, Tolstoy and others.
collections.intro: Photographs let us look into the eyes of people who lived long ago. These portraits show writers, inventors, leaders and rebels as they really looked.

collections.name: Faces of Freedom
collections.blurb: Douglass, Truth, Tubman, Parks, Robinson and the March on Washington.
collections.intro: People who fought for freedom and equality, from a man who escaped slavery to the crowds who marched on Washington.

collections.name: City Lights and Skyscrapers
collections.blurb: From horse-drawn streets to the Empire State Building.
collections.intro: As cities grew taller and busier, photographers followed. Stieglitz, Strand, Abbott and Hine showed how new skyscrapers and crowds changed the way people lived.

collections.name: Wars and Their Aftermath
collections.blurb: From the Crimean War to D-Day.
collections.intro: Photographers have followed armies since 1855. These pictures show soldiers, ruins and the moments when wars ended, and some are hard to look at.

collections.name: To the Moon
collections.blurb: The Moon, from Apollo to Orion.
collections.intro: People have looked at the Moon for as long as there have been people. These photographs show the Moon up close, from the first Apollo pictures to the newest spacecraft.
